t.utah beach@49.4,-1.2:
Low dunes, a wide grey-gold beach and a sky that seems to go on forever: the westernmost of the D-Day landing beaches looks peaceful today. On 6 June 1944, troops of the US 4th Infantry Division came ashore here, on the eastern coast of the Cotentin peninsula, after paratroopers had dropped inland during the night. A current pushed the first landing craft south of their intended sector, onto a less defended stretch of sand, and Brigadier General Theodore Roosevelt Jr., walking the beach with a cane, decided to start the war from right there. Casualties at Utah were far lower than at Omaha, a few kilometres to the east.

The beach is part of Sainte-Marie-du-Mont, and the Utah Beach museum stands on the site of a German bunker, with landing craft, vehicles and a B-26 bomber inside. Memorials line the dunes. Inland, Sainte-Mère-Église was one of the first towns liberated, and it is famous for the paratrooper whose parachute caught on the church tower; a dummy still hangs there today. Across the bay to the east, the cliffs of Pointe du Hoc and the beaches of Omaha are visible on clear days.

The landscape behind the beach is the marsh of the Cotentin, flat and wet, crossed by causeways that were bitterly fought over in 1944 because the Germans had flooded the fields around them. The riding is easy and atmospheric: narrow lanes between hedgerows, small stone villages and long straight roads across the marshes. Wind off the Channel can be strong and it rains often, but the light after a shower is beautiful. Traffic peaks in June around the anniversary, when vintage jeeps and re-enactors fill the roads.

Fuel is limited near the beach; Carentan, fifteen kilometres away, is the reliable option, and Sainte-Mère-Église has shops and cafés. Normandy food is all about dairy and apples: butter and cream from Isigny, camembert, cider and calvados, the apple brandy. Seafood is excellent along the coast, from oysters to mussels. Take time on the beach itself, walk to the waterline and look back at the dunes. It is a short distance, but it was a long way for the men who crossed it.
t.beaches of the d day landings@49.4,-0.7:
Port-en-Bessin is a working fishing harbour squeezed into a gap in the cliffs, and on the morning of 6 June 1944 it sat exactly on the seam between Omaha Beach to the west and Gold Beach to the east. British commandos took the port in the days that followed, linking the American and British sectors. Today the trawlers still come in with scallops in season, the boats crowd the inner basin, and a stubby stone tower designed by Vauban's engineers watches over the entrance. It is a fine base for exploring the whole stretch of the Normandy landing beaches.

The coast road, the D514, runs west towards Colleville-sur-Mer and the American Cemetery above Omaha, where nearly ten thousand white crosses and stars stand in rows on a lawn above the sea. East lies Longues-sur-Mer, where the German coastal battery still has its guns in place in their concrete casemates, and beyond it Arromanches, with the remains of the Mulberry artificial harbour scattered across the bay like a broken necklace. Each place has a different feel, and it is worth giving at least a day to the area.

Inland, Bayeux is ten minutes away. It was the first town of note liberated and escaped serious damage, so its cathedral and medieval streets survive. It is also home to the Bayeux Tapestry, the embroidered story of an earlier cross-Channel invasion in 1066, which makes a curious and moving counterpoint to the beaches.

The riding is gentle and scenic rather than technical. The D514 rolls along the top of the cliffs and dips into small villages, with long sightlines and views of the sea, while the lanes inland wind between hedgerows, the famous bocage that made the fighting after D-Day so brutal. Summer brings heavy traffic, coaches and camper vans, and the anniversary period in early June gets very busy. Spring and early autumn are calmer. The weather changes fast; rain showers blow in from the Channel, and wind on the cliff tops can be strong.

Port-en-Bessin has restaurants serving seafood and a few shops, and you will find fuel at the supermarkets around Bayeux. Try the local cider and calvados, but save them for the evening. Above all, take your time and walk on the sand for a while.
t.omaha beach@49.4,-0.9:
The coast here is long, shallow and sandy, backed by low bluffs, and on the morning of 6 June 1944 it became one of the most terrible places in the history of the Second World War. Omaha was the code name given to a stretch of beach in the Allied landings in Normandy, assigned to American troops, and it was the hardest of the five beaches: the German defences on the bluffs were strong, the bombardment had missed many positions, and the tide and weather scattered the landing craft. Thousands of men were killed or wounded on the sand and the shingle in the first hours, though by evening the beachhead held.

The Normandy American Cemetery at Colleville-sur-Mer, on the bluff above the beach, holds nearly ten thousand graves in rows of white marble crosses and Stars of David, with a view over the sea, and the site is quiet and moving. Nearby, the cliff at Pointe du Hoc, where American Rangers scaled the rock under fire, still shows the craters left by the bombing. Concrete bunkers and gun emplacements remain along the coast, many covered in grass, and the museums at Saint-Laurent-sur-Mer and Bayeux tell the story in detail.

Today the beach is calm, with walkers, horse riders and families flying kites at low tide, and the contrast with its past is strange. The coast road, the D514, runs close to the shore through a string of villages, with views over the water, and is a pleasant, easy ride at moderate speed. It becomes busy in summer and especially around the anniversary in early June, when veterans, ceremonies and crowds fill the area. Respect is expected at memorials, so keep your helmet off and your voice low, and park in official areas.

Port-en-Bessin and Grandcamp-Maisy have fuel and small restaurants, but for larger choice head to Bayeux, about sixteen kilometres away, which has stations, supermarkets and hotels, and the famous medieval tapestry. Normandy offers apples in every form: cider, calvados, tarts, and creamy cheeses such as camembert and pont-l'évêque. The weather changes quickly on the coast, so pack a waterproof, and check the tides before walking on the beach.
t.juno beach@49.3,-0.4:
On the morning of 6 June 1944 the Canadian 3rd Infantry Division landed here, between Courseulles-sur-Mer and Saint-Aubin-sur-Mer, in the middle of the five Normandy landing beaches. Rough seas delayed the first wave, so the troops arrived after the naval bombardment had lifted and the German defenders had recovered. The fighting on the sea wall and in the seaside villages was fierce, and Canadian casualties that day were heavy, but by evening the division had pushed further inland than any other Allied force. Today the beach is a long, quiet strand of sand, with low dunes, villas with shuttered windows, and a few concrete bunkers still half-buried at the water's edge.

The Juno Beach Centre at Courseulles, opened in 2003, tells the Canadian story with clarity and warmth, and the guides are often young Canadians on summer placements. A short walk away, a bunker preserved from the Atlantic Wall stands behind the dunes, and the villages along the shore keep their wartime stories in street names and small memorials. Courseulles is also known for its oysters and whelks, which are sold from stalls near the harbour, and a plate of them with a glass of Normandy cider is a good lunch.

The coast road is gentle and flat, running between the villages along the English Channel, with long views of the sea and a hedge-lined landscape inland. It gets busy in July and August, with cars and cyclists, and the best time to ride is early morning or late in the day. Surfaces are generally good. For something more varied, the Bocage inland offers narrow lanes with high banks and farmland. Rain can come in from the sea quickly, so carry a waterproof layer.

Courseulles-sur-Mer has about four thousand people and has fuel and bakeries, while Douvres-la-Délivrande, six kilometres inland, is a bit larger and has supermarkets. Arromanches and its remains of the Mulberry artificial harbour lie to the east along the coast and make an easy second stop. Bring something to read, take your time, and let the quiet of the beach sink in. It rewards people who arrive without a schedule.
t.royal water temple pura taman ayun@-8.5,:
Pura Taman Ayun means the temple of the beautiful garden, and it is a royal temple surrounded by a wide moat. The rajas of Mengwi built it in 1634, as the main temple of their small kingdom, and the broad lawns, canals and pavilions give it the air of a palace garden as much as a shrine. Across the inner courtyard rise the merus, shrines with tiered thatched roofs of black ijuk fibre, some with as many as eleven levels, which represent mountains and the homes of the gods. The temple lies in the middle of a district of rice fields, and it is part of the Subak cultural landscape that UNESCO listed in 2012, because the water for those fields is managed by village irrigation societies, the subak, which have been sharing it for a thousand years.

You can see the system at work in the countryside around. Water runs from the crater lakes down through canals, tunnels and little weirs, and each farmer gets a share fixed by custom and by the priests of the water temples. The rice terraces step down the slopes in curves, and the whole landscape looks both natural and designed. Ubud, a little to the north-east, is better known for its artists and cafes, and Tabanan, close by, is a market town in the middle of Bali's rice bowl.

The riding in Bali is a lively business. Roads are narrow, crowded with scooters, trucks and temple processions, and the surface is often cracked or flooded. Traffic keeps to the left. Dogs, chickens and offerings of flowers and rice lie in the road, and you should not run over the offerings if you can help it. You need a licence valid for motorcycles in Indonesia, and the police do check. The best riding is in the early morning, when the air is cool and the rice fields glitter, and the dry season, May to September, is easier than the wet.

Fuel is sold at petrol stations in Tabanan and Denpasar, and at roadside stalls in glass bottles. Dress modestly for the temple and wear a sash, which is lent at the entrance, and move around the grounds quietly. Mengwi is a short ride from the coast, and the sunset at Tanah Lot, a sea temple on a rock, is a short drive west. Try a plate of nasi campur and a fresh coconut, and watch the ducks being herded through the paddies.
t.forest steppe part of daursky snbr@50.4,:
Dauria is the name for the open steppe where Siberia runs into Mongolia and China, and it is one of the last great undisturbed grasslands in Asia. The reserve called Daursky protects a slice of it in the far south of Zabaykalsky Krai, in an area of rolling hills, shallow salt lakes, and a sky that feels twice as large as normal. Forest steppe is the term for the zone where patches of larch and birch push out into the grass, and here the mixture is dry, windy and bright, with long winters of fierce cold and short summers that can be surprisingly hot.

The great attraction is the birdlife. The Torey lakes, which fill and dry in a cycle of years, are a major stopover for migrating waterfowl, and the steppe is the breeding ground for cranes, including the white-naped and the Daurian, which have a hoarse, rolling call that carries for miles. Mongolian gazelles cross the frontier in huge herds, sometimes in the thousands, and the marmot, called tarbagan, sits upright beside its burrow and whistles. The sound of the place is wind, birds and very little else. The Chuh-Nuur lake cluster in the label is part of the same wetland landscape, shared with Mongolia and China.

This is, by any standard, a remote ride. The nearest village is Nizhniy Tsasuchey, about twenty kilometres away, with just over three thousand people, and the roads in the area range from poor asphalt to dirt tracks that turn to mud after rain. Because the area is in a border zone, special permits are required, and the rules on entry, photography and travel change, so inquire well ahead. Do not wander toward the frontier. It is also worth checking the current rules for travel in Russia before making any plans.

Fuel is scarce, and the supplies of any kind are thin, so carry spare fuel, water, food and tools. Mosquitoes and ticks are fierce in early summer, and storms can build quickly on the open plain. The reward is the silence, the huge horizon and the evening light, which turns the grass copper.
t.comoe national park@9.0,-4.0:
Comoe National Park is one of the largest protected areas in West Africa, more than a million hectares in the north-east corner of Cote d'Ivoire, and it is built around a river that does something unexpected. The Comoe flows through savanna country, but along its banks it supports strips of dense gallery forest, in a way that lets forest animals and plants reach far north into the grassland. The result is an unusual mix of habitats and a wide range of wildlife, and the park was added to the World Heritage list in 1983.

The animals include elephants, hippos, buffalo, many antelope species and a population of chimpanzees that is known for using tools. Lions and leopards remain, though they are seen rarely, and the birds, from fish eagles to hornbills, are abundant. The park suffered badly from poaching and instability in the 1990s and 2000s and was placed on the danger list, then recovered enough to be taken off it in 2017, but the situation can change, so it is wise to ask about conditions. The best time for wildlife is the dry season, from December to March, when the grass is low and the animals gather at the river.

The ride to Comoe passes through the old trading land of the north, and the label links it to Kong, a town that was once the centre of an important Muslim kingdom in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Kong's great mosque, built in the Sudanese style with mud walls, wooden beams projecting from the surface and tapering buttresses, is one of the finest of the region. It sits among old houses and trees, and the sense of age is strong. Roads in the north vary from good tarmac to red laterite tracks, which turn to slick mud in the rains from May to October.

The north is hot, and the harmattan wind in winter brings dust. Check the security situation in the border areas before you go, arrange permits and guides in advance, and expect to be treated with courtesy at the checkpoints.
t.mount huangshan@30.1,118.2:
Huangshan, the Yellow Mountain, rises in the south of Anhui province from a flat region of tea fields and villages, and its granite peaks, gnarled pines and seas of cloud have made it one of the most painted mountains in China. The highest of its seventy-two peaks, Lotus Peak, stands at about 1,864 metres. What makes the mountain special is the combination of tall, sharp, bare rock and the pine trees that grow out of the cracks, shaped by wind and weather into strange, twisted forms, each of which has a name, such as the Welcoming Guest Pine. UNESCO listed it in 1990.

The mountain is famous for four things, which the Chinese call the four wonders: the pines, the odd-shaped rocks, the sea of clouds and the hot springs. The clouds are the biggest draw, and on a good morning, the valleys fill with white mist and the peaks stand out like islands. Sunrise from one of the summits, with the first light touching the granite, is the classic experience, and people get up in the dark to see it. The weather is unpredictable, with fog and rain on many days, and winter brings snow and ice, which add to the beauty but make the stone steps hazardous.

Visitors reach the summit by cable car or by climbing thousands of stone steps, and many stay overnight in the hotels on top to see the sunrise. There are no roads on the mountain, so motorbikes are irrelevant here, and the ride on the approach is to the foot of the mountain. At its base, the villages of Xidi and Hongcun, with their white-walled, black-tiled houses, ponds and carved wooden gates, belong to the Huizhou culture of merchants and scholars, and are a World Heritage Site in their own right. The surrounding hills produce the famous Huangshan Maofeng green tea.

The nearest big town is not listed here, and I would rather not guess. Fuel and food are available in the tourist town at the foot, and foreign riders in China are subject to strict rules, so most people arrive by bus or train. Come in spring or autumn, bring warm and waterproof clothing, and expect crowds in holidays.
t.changzhou city section of jiangnan canal:
Changzhou does not appear on many bucket lists, which is a pity, because it holds a living stretch of the Grand Canal, the longest man-made waterway in the world. The canal here is the Jiangnan section, the southern part that links the Yangtze with Hangzhou, and it runs right through the city, past old lanes, stone bridges and modern towers. UNESCO added the Grand Canal to its list in 2014, and Changzhou's urban section is one of the segments that make up the listing.

What makes it interesting is that it is still in use. Barges loaded with sand and gravel still move slowly along the water, while the banks have been turned into promenades and parks. The waterway has been dug, widened and rerouted many times over the centuries, and what you see is the product of all those efforts. Tianning Pagoda, a modern rebuilding of a temple tower, is among the tallest in China and can be seen from far off. The poet Su Dongpo, one of the great figures of the Song dynasty, spent his last days in Changzhou in 1101, and the city remembers him in street names and a memorial.

Changzhou is a big industrial city of nearly a million people, the sort that makes machines, textiles and, more recently, electric vehicles and batteries. Traffic is dense, with scooters, buses and trucks, and the region is flat and densely populated, so there is little in the way of scenic riding. If you travel by motorbike in China, be aware that foreign licences are not valid and many cities limit motorcycles, so check the situation well ahead and think about hiring a car or taking local transport instead.

Practicalities are simple in a city this size: fuel stations, shops, hotels and restaurants are everywhere. Spring and autumn offer pleasant weather, while summer is hot and sticky, and plum rains in June soak the region. Jiangnan food is delicate and a bit sweet, with canal fish, river shrimp and noodles in broth. Walk the canal path in the evening, when the lights come on along the water and people gather to dance, play cards and fish, and you will see why a working waterway can still feel like the heart of a city.
t.suqian section of zhong canal@34.0,118.2:
The Zhong Canal, the Middle Canal, was dug in the late seventeenth century for a very practical reason: the Yellow River kept getting in the way. Boats on the Grand Canal had to cross that unruly river in northern Jiangsu, and the crossing was dangerous and often blocked by floods and silt. Engineers of the Qing dynasty cut a new channel that avoided the worst of it, and the Suqian section is a reminder of that effort. It belongs to the Grand Canal's UNESCO listing, and the canal here is a broad, working waterway with barges, embankments and farmland on either side.

Suqian is an old crossroads between the Yellow River's former courses, the Yi and Shu rivers and the great lakes of northern Jiangsu, and the land is flat and watery, with poplar-lined roads, paddy fields and ponds. The city is famous in China for its baijiu, strong grain liquor, which comes in well-known brands, and it is also traditionally linked with Xiang Yu, the warrior who contested the throne with Liu Bang after the fall of the Qin. Emperor Qianlong, who loved touring the south, is said to have rested at a temple palace by the Yellow River near here.

For riding, the plain is relaxed but visually repetitive. Roads are straight, wide and busy with trucks, and speed enforcement by camera is common. The pleasure is in watching local life at the margins: fishermen, boats with laundry hung out, brick kilns and orchards. Foreign visitors on motorbikes face licensing problems in China, so check carefully, and keep in mind that signs are mainly in Chinese. A taxi or a hired driver will make the visit easier.

The nearest sizeable town in the data is Suicheng, about 25 km away, with around 60,000 people, and Suqian city has plenty of fuel and food. Late spring and autumn are the best seasons. Winters are cold and damp, and summers are hot and humid, with thunderstorms. Local food includes river fish, braised dishes and pancakes, and sharing a table with a small glass of the local spirit is the usual way to end a meal. The canal at dusk, with the water turning copper, is the thing to remember.
t.cordouan lighthouse@45.6,-1.2:
Cordouan is a lighthouse standing alone on a rock bank in the mouth of the Gironde estuary, seven kilometres or so out to sea, and you cannot ride to it. What the coordinates show is the point on the coast opposite, with the resort of Saint-Palais-sur-Mer nearly nine kilometres off and Royan, a town of nineteen thousand, a bit farther. The lighthouse is a boat trip away from Royan or from the Médoc side at Le Verdon-sur-Mer, and only in season and when the tide and swell permit.

The tower is one of the most remarkable buildings in France: a Renaissance and later palace of a lighthouse, begun under Henri III by the architect Louis de Foix at the end of the sixteenth century and raised in height in the late eighteenth. It has a chapel, a royal apartment and an elaborate stone interior that looks more like a château than a navigation aid. It is sometimes called the Versailles of the sea. The Gironde mouth is a dangerous place, with shifting sandbanks, strong tides and violent weather, and generations of keepers lived out here in all conditions.

For a rider, the coast here is a charming sprawl of seaside towns, pine woods and dunes, with the estuary on one side and the Atlantic on the other. The roads through the forests of the Côte de Beauté are quiet, flat and shaded, with sandy edges, and in summer they fill with holiday traffic, bicycles and the slow crawl to the beaches. Early morning or September is the time to go. Wind off the ocean is constant, and storms in autumn can be brutal.

Royan was heavily bombed in the last months of the Second World War and rebuilt in a bold modernist style, with a concrete church that is worth a look. It has fuel, restaurants and a long beach. Oysters from nearby Marennes-Oléron are the local pride, and a plate of them with a glass of white wine is a fine reward after a salty day.
t.area of low dam on the plain causeway in:
Five thousand years ago, a society on the Yangtze delta built dams. The Liangzhu culture, which flourished around 3300 to 2300 BC in what is now Zhejiang province, built a huge water management system in the hills and plain northwest of modern Hangzhou, and UNESCO listed it in 2019 together with the ruins of the Liangzhu city. The system included high dams in the mountains, low dams on the plain and a network of canals and reservoirs, and it is among the oldest large-scale hydraulic engineering works known.

The low dams on the plain were made of layers of clay and grass bundles, and some are still visible as low ridges in the fields. They controlled floods, stored water and provided transport routes for boats. The scale is hard to grasp, because the system covers a wide area of paddy fields and low hills, but archaeologists have mapped it in detail. It came to light not long ago, in the early 2000s, and the dating shows that the engineering predates the first known Chinese dynasties by many centuries.

The landscape is gentle and green, a patchwork of rice fields, bamboo groves, tea terraces and small canals. The air is humid, and the climate is subtropical, with hot, wet summers and a rainy spring. The best time to ride is autumn, when the air is clear and the temperature mild. Roads are well surfaced, and traffic is heavy near Hangzhou, a city of more than six million people that sits about twenty kilometres away and has everything a traveller needs, including fuel.

Deqing, a smaller town to the north, is famous for Moganshan, a mountain resort with bamboo forests. As elsewhere in China, foreign riders face restrictions on riding a motorcycle, so check the rules in advance. If you are visiting, bring a hat and water, and give yourself time to walk the fields. The landscape is subtle, and you need to look carefully to see the humps and ridges that mark the old dams.
t.shangqiu xiayi section of tongji canal@3:
The Tongji Canal was one of the great works of the Sui dynasty, dug in the early seventh century as part of the Grand Canal. The emperor Yang ordered it built to link the Yellow River with the Huai River, and it carried grain, soldiers and tribute across the plain for centuries. At its height, it was the main artery between the north and the rich Yangtze delta. It silted up and was abandoned after the Song dynasty, and parts of it were buried under farmland. UNESCO listed the surviving sections as part of the Grand Canal in 2014.

Shangqiu, in eastern Henan, has a very long history. It was a capital of the Shang people, early in Chinese history, and later an important city on the canal. The Xiayi section, and the site at Liuzi, are places where archaeologists have exposed the old channel. What you see is a broad depression in the field, with banks and the remains of a wharf or a lock, and information boards explaining what it was. It is a modest sight, but it shows how a canal that carried an empire has faded into the farmland.

The surrounding plain is very flat and very fertile, a land of wheat, maize, sesame and sweet potatoes, laced with irrigation channels and poplar windbreaks. Villages are brick built, and there are small temples and graves among the fields. Summer is hot and humid, and winter is cold and dry, with fog common. Roads are straight, and traffic is mostly trucks, farm tractors and three-wheeled carts. Dust from harvested fields is common in autumn.

The nearest town of any size is Bozhou, in neighbouring Anhui province, with about a hundred and seventy thousand people, while Shangqiu has fuel, hotels and restaurants. Bozhou is famous for traditional Chinese medicine and for a strong spirit made from sorghum. As in all of China, foreign visitors should check the local rules before bringing a motorcycle. Come in spring, when the fields are bright green, or in autumn, when the maize is gold. The canal is hard to see, but it is a good reason to slow down.
t.megaliths of carnac and of the shores of:
The fields at Carnac look like a parade ground that someone forgot to dismiss. Thousands of standing stones, grey and lichen-streaked, stand in long parallel rows across the heath, running for more than a kilometre in the great alignments at Ménec, Kermario and Kerlescan. They were put up in the Neolithic, several thousand years before the Romans, and nobody knows exactly why. Astronomy, burial and ritual have all been proposed, and a Breton legend offers a quicker answer: Saint Cornély, chased by Roman soldiers, turned them into stone. The wider area of the Morbihan, with its tombs, dolmens and tumuli, has recently been listed by UNESCO.

The sheer scale is what stays with you. Alongside the rows stand huge burial mounds such as the Tumulus Saint-Michel, topped by a small chapel, and dozens of single stones in fields and gardens that locals have lived around for generations. In the high season, access to the main alignments is restricted to guided visits and a fence keeps visitors off the grass, which has suffered from erosion, so expect to look from the path in summer. Out of season the fences open and the stones can be walked among.

The riding is gentle, flat and best taken at a dawdle. Roads thread between pine woods, salt marshes and little harbours, with long views over the Gulf of Morbihan and its islands. In July and August the area is overrun with caravans and cyclists, and the road along the Quiberon peninsula has long queues. Early morning or the shoulder seasons are much better. Auray, on the river of the same name, has over twelve thousand people and is the best place for fuel and a meal. Carnac and Plouharnel have stations too, but they get crowded in summer.

Eat oysters, pancakes with salted butter caramel, and the butter cake called kouign-amann, which locals say can only be made properly in Brittany. A cider from a Breton producer goes well with all of them.

The weather is mild and changeable, and the Atlantic sends in showers at any time. May, June and September give the best balance of light, warmth and quiet.
t.presqu ile de quiberon bassin de kerboul:
Quiberon is a thin finger of granite that points south into the Atlantic from the Breton coast, fourteen kilometres long and in places hardly a couple of hundred metres wide. The Bassin de Kerboul in this label lies on the mainland side of the peninsula around Saint-Pierre-Quiberon, a patch of sheltered water and marsh edge behind the dunes, and I would rather say that than invent a particular spot. What I know for certain is the shape of the place: one side, the Baie de Quiberon, is calm and shelves gently; the other, the Côte Sauvage, is wild, with long Atlantic swells smashing into black rocks.

The way in is a narrow causeway, a tombolo, where the road and a single railway line squeeze between dunes and sea at Penthièvre, guarded by a fort that has been a prison and a battlefield. It was here in 1795 that émigré royalists, landed by British ships, were defeated by Republican troops under Hoche, and the story is still told with feeling. Earlier, in 1759, the great naval battle of Quiberon Bay was fought off these shores, where the British fleet defeated the French in a gale, one of the turning points of the Seven Years' War.

On a motorbike this is a joyous place in the right season. The D768 down the middle is straight and fast, and the narrow lanes toward the coast twist among low stone houses with blue shutters. In July and August it is overrun, and the one road in and out can crawl, so go in May, June or September, or early in the day. Wind is the major factor: gusts across the isthmus can be severe, and the Côte Sauvage has no barriers worth the name, so keep back from edges.

Nearby Carnac, with its thousands of standing stones, lies a short ride away. Quiberon is where the salted-butter caramel was supposedly invented, and its sardine canneries made the town rich; you will find tins in the shops. Quiberon town, with about five thousand people, has fuel, restaurants and the ferries to Belle-Île, Houat and Hoëdic, and Saint-Pierre-Quiberon has a smaller supply of shops. Fill the tank before you reach the causeway if you can, because queues for the stations in high summer can be long.
t.comoe national park@9.1,-3.8:
Comoé is the largest national park in West Africa, an enormous block of savanna and forest in the northeast of Côte d'Ivoire, and its name comes from the river that runs through it. The Comoé keeps flowing in the dry season when nearly everything else dries up, and thanks to it, strips of dense gallery forest push deep into open grassland. The result is a mixture of habitats where forest animals and savanna animals share the same space, which is rare, and was one reason the park gained world heritage status in 1983.

The wildlife is serious but shy. Elephants, buffalo, hippos, several species of antelope and many monkeys live here, and the park is known for chimpanzees that build nests in the savanna woodland rather than the deep forest. Lions and leopards exist, though you would be lucky to see them. Birdlife is rich, with hornbills, kingfishers and raptors. The park suffered badly from poaching during the years of conflict in the early 2000s, and was put on UNESCO's danger list, though conservation efforts have improved and it was removed in 2017.

This is rough-country riding. Tracks inside the park are laterite and sand, rutted after rain and dusty in the dry season, and the nearest paved roads are some distance away. The best period is the dry season from about December to March, when animals gather by the water and grass is lower. The rainy season makes many tracks impassable. Come with a capable bike, spare fuel, plenty of water and repair kit, and ideally a guide, since mobile signal is thin.

Fuel is not available in the park, and the towns around it, such as Bouna, may have unreliable supply, so carry extra. On the way back through Kong, the old trading town, look for the Great Mosque, a wonderful example of Sudano-Sahelian mud architecture, with buttressed walls and wooden beams that stick out like pins.
t.qingkou complex@33.4,118.9:
Qingkou is the place where China's engineers tried, for centuries, to make two very different rivers behave. Here, near Huai'an in northern Jiangsu, the Grand Canal met the Huai River, and from the twelfth century until the middle of the nineteenth, the Yellow River also took over the Huai's lower course, bringing enormous loads of silt. The canal crossed this unstable junction, and getting boats safely across it, while controlling floods and keeping the water level right, was among the hardest tasks in the entire waterway.

The Qingkou complex is a group of sites related to that struggle: locks, sluices, embankments and guide walls, built and rebuilt through the Ming and Qing dynasties. The water control here was so important that senior officials were stationed in Huai'an, and the emperors Kangxi and Qianlong made inspection tours of the area. It is part of the Grand Canal's UNESCO listing from 2014, and gives a sense of how much human effort went into moving grain and salt along these channels. Today it is not a showy place, but a landscape of waterways, banks and old stonework, set among fields and villages.

Huai'an itself has a place in modern history as the home town of Zhou Enlai, the first premier of the People's Republic, and its old centre along the canal has been restored. The countryside is flat, wet and green, with rice paddies and fishponds, and the roads are straight and busy with trucks and farm vehicles. Winter can be cold and damp, spring brings rain and summer is very hot and humid, so autumn offers the most comfortable days. Foreigners riding motorcycles in China should check permit and licence rules thoroughly before they plan a trip.

Huai'an, a large city about twenty-four kilometres from the site, has fuel stations, restaurants and hotels. The local cuisine of the Huai'an area is known for freshwater fish, crayfish and soft-shelled turtle dishes, and the lotus root soup is a gentle pleasure. Bring water, take a map with Chinese place names, and plan a leisurely day.
t.daursky snbr and valley of dzeren nature:
Dauria is a grassland that does not care about borders. Here, where Russia's Zabaykalsky region meets Mongolia and China, the steppe rolls away in pale gold waves toward the horizon, broken by salt lakes and low hills. The name on this point stands for two Russian reserves, the Daursky Biosphere Reserve and the Valley of Dzeren, which together with the Mongolian reserves nearby form a protected landscape recognised by UNESCO in 2017. Dzeren is the Mongolian gazelle, a pale, fast antelope, and the valley is named after the herds that come and go across the frontier in search of better grass.

The lakes are the secret to the place. Torey Lake and its neighbours fill and dry out in cycles that last many years, and the shifting water level pushes the whole ecosystem back and forth. When water is high, the shores are a major stopover for migrating birds, among them white-naped cranes, swan geese and great bustards. When the lakes shrink, the dry bed turns into salt flats and the birds move on. It is landscape as a slow pulse, and it makes any visit different from the last. The area is also associated with the early life of the Mongol ruler Genghis Khan, who is said to have been born near the Onon river not far to the north.

Riding here means tracks more than roads. Surfaces are sand, gravel and hard steppe soil, which is easy in dry weather and slippery after rain, and the winds are a serious factor, often strong all afternoon. Summers are warm with sudden storms, and winters are severely cold, dropping far below freezing. The best weeks are in late spring and early autumn, when migratory birds are around and the grass is either green or golden. Because this is a border zone, permits are required for entering the reserve and areas near the frontier, so contact the reserve office and arrange everything beforehand.

Supplies are limited. Small towns such as Nizhny Tsasuchey and the larger Borzya offer fuel and food, but you should carry extra petrol and water, and tell someone where you are going. In return you get skies that go on forever, the smell of wormwood and warm grass, and the odd sight of a herd of gazelles pouring over a ridge at a gallop.
t.labuan bajo@-8.5,119.9:
Labuan Bajo was a sleepy fishing village not so long ago, and it is still trying to catch up with its own fame. It sits at the western tip of Flores, in eastern Indonesia, facing a scatter of dry brown islands that rise from a bright blue sea, and it is the gateway to Komodo National Park, a UNESCO site since 1991, home of the Komodo dragon. The largest living lizard on earth, which can grow to about three metres, survives in the wild only on a few islands here, and boat trips from the harbour take visitors to see them on Komodo and Rinca.

The town is bright with the paint of new hotels and dive shops, and the harbour is crowded with wooden boats waiting for the morning tourists. The waters around are famously rich, with manta rays, reef sharks and fast currents that bring a huge amount of marine life past the islands, and divers come from around the world. In the evening the waterfront is the place to be, as the sun sinks behind the islands in streaks of orange and the smell of grilled fish drifts from the night stalls.

For riders, this is the western end of the Trans-Flores Highway, a road that crosses the island for roughly seven hundred kilometres toward Maumere. It begins gently, with a climb out of town into dry hills and then green valleys, but the sections ahead are long and winding. The surface is mostly paved, though potholes, landslides and loose stones appear without warning, and the corners are tight, with buses and trucks taking up more than their share. Take daylight hours seriously, since night riding with animals and unlit vehicles is hazardous. Heat and humidity are constant, with a dry season from about May to October that makes the road easiest.

Fuel is available in town, and you should fill the tank and carry water before heading east, as villages on the way have small stations that may run dry. Guesthouses and restaurants are plentiful, with fresh seafood as the best choice, and a morning coffee from Flores beans is highly recommended. Remember that Indonesian traffic drives on the left, and that people are generally kind to foreign riders, so a smile and a wave solve many problems.
t.coos bay@43.4,-124.2:
Coos Bay is a working harbour on the Oregon coast, and the working is visible. Stacks of timber and wood chips wait on the docks, ships load cargo, and the town's main street faces the water, with a mixture of old brick buildings and low modern shops. About sixteen thousand people live here, making it the largest city on the Oregon coast, and the bay itself is the largest natural harbour between San Francisco and the Columbia river, a fact that drove the logging and shipping industries for more than a century. A slow decline in timber has pushed the town to find other ways to earn a living.

A graceful steel bridge crosses the entrance to the bay on Highway 101, the McCullough Memorial Bridge, designed by Conde McCullough, who built many of the coast's bridges in the 1930s in an elegant art deco style. Just south of town, the Oregon Dunes National Recreation Area stretches for about sixty kilometres along the coast, one of the largest areas of coastal sand dunes in North America, with towering sand hills, forest islands and lakes. Farther west, at Cape Arago, sea lions bark on the rocks and the cliffs drop to the surf, while the Shore Acres gardens, on a former estate, are known for their flowers.

For riders, Highway 101 is an easy and scenic road. North of Coos Bay it runs through the dunes and forest toward Florence, with views of the sea and a good surface, and south it passes through cranberry bog country near Bandon, with its rocky sea stacks, to the Redwood coast of California. Fog and drizzle are common, particularly in summer mornings, and the Pacific air is cool, so carry a waterproof layer. Logging trucks use the road, and tourists in RVs go slowly, so be patient on the bends. Spring and early autumn have the best weather.

Fuel, food and lodging are available in town, and the seafood is outstanding, with Dungeness crab, fish and chips and oysters. At dusk, the fog rolls in over the dunes and the sound of foghorns drifts across the water, which gives the whole coast a haunting atmosphere.
t.canal site at liuzi@33.8,116.6:
The plains of eastern Henan and northern Anhui are among the flattest and most densely farmed in the world, a patchwork of wheat, maize and villages, strung together by poplar-lined lanes and straight roads. This was the heartland of old China, and the Grand Canal ran through it. The section here, the Liuzi canal site, belongs to the Tongji Canal, built in the Sui dynasty in the early seventh century to link the Yellow River with the Huai and eventually the Yangtze. It was dug by labour on a vast scale and became the main artery for grain, taxes and troops moving between north and south for several hundred years.

The Grand Canal as a whole is a staggering thing, almost eighteen hundred kilometres of waterway from Beijing to Hangzhou, assembled from many sections built over more than a thousand years, and UNESCO listed it in 2014. The Tongji Canal fell out of use after the Yellow River, which has a habit of shifting its course and flooding, buried it in silt, and archaeologists have since excavated sections to find the old banks, wharves and even wrecked boats. At a site like this one, you see a low dip in the field, an excavated bank, a display board and a view across farmland, and if you use your imagination you can hear the barges.

The roads in this region are straight, flat and busy, running between villages that seem to blend into one another. Trucks, tractors and three-wheeled carts share the carriageway, and local driving is a game that requires attention. In wheat harvest, around early June, grain is spread to dry on the road itself, and in autumn, burning of crop residue can produce smoke. Scenery is rural China at close quarters, with old men on benches, children on bicycles and a good many dogs.

Suixi, about eighteen kilometres away with seventy-four thousand people, has fuel, simple restaurants and hotels. The local food is noodles, steamed buns and lamb soup, and tea is served strong. Foreign riders in China face strict rules about licences and permits, so arrange everything in advance. Spring and autumn are the best times, with clear air and mild temperatures, while summer is hot, humid and stormy, and winter is cold and dusty.
t.shangqiu nanguan section of tongji canal:
The name Shangqiu is one of the oldest in Chinese history. This was the heartland of the Shang people, whose dynasty ruled the Yellow River plain more than three thousand years ago, and a persistent tradition says that the Shang were such good traders that their name became the word for merchants and commerce, shang. Whether or not the etymology is exact, the town has a good claim to being the cradle of trade. Later, under the Song dynasty, Shangqiu was one of the secondary capitals, known as the Southern Capital, and a major hub for grain, salt and silk.

The Nanguan section of the Tongji Canal runs by the south gate of the old city, and it was here that boats from the south unloaded rice and goods for the northern markets. Part of the old bank and wharf has been excavated, and a short stretch has been preserved and interpreted for visitors. Looking at a ditch beside a neat modern park, you may wonder why this is a World Heritage site, but it helps to remember that the canal carried a large share of the empire's grain, and that the whole network is listed as one of the great works of hydraulic engineering in history.

Shangqiu itself is a rather quiet city of about a hundred and eighty thousand, with an old walled town, well restored in recent years, and a tradition of folk culture, local opera and flatbreads. The roads in the area are flat, straight and often tree-lined, and they connect villages and market towns in a regular grid. Truck traffic and agricultural vehicles share them with cars. There is little in the way of dramatic riding, but a lot of daily life to see: wheat drying on the tarmac in June, old men playing chess in the shade, vendors selling steamed buns.

Fuel stations are easy to find, and restaurants serve noodles, dumplings and Henan stews. Heat and humidity are severe in July and August, with heavy rain, and winter brings cold, dry air and dust. Spring and autumn are the best seasons. Foreign riders in China need to comply with strict rules about licences, vehicles and guides, so check ahead and arrange permits in advance, because police checkpoints are common and rules are enforced.
t.taierzhuang section of zhong canal@34.6,:
Taierzhuang is a canal town that was destroyed and rebuilt. In the spring of 1938 it was the scene of one of the first major Chinese victories over the invading Japanese army, a battle fought house by house through the streets for weeks, and the town was reduced to rubble. The victory was a great morale booster at a dark time. Decades later, the town was reconstructed in the style of the old canal towns, with grey brick houses, stone bridges and tiled roofs, and today it is a popular heritage destination, with a long lantern-lit waterfront.

The canal that runs through it is the Zhong Canal, the middle section of the Grand Canal, which was dug and improved between the Yuan and Ming dynasties to carry grain from the south to Beijing. The Grand Canal is almost eighteen hundred kilometres long and is considered the longest man-made waterway on earth, and UNESCO listed it in 2014. Taierzhuang was a stopping place where boats waited for a favourable wind or paid dues, and in its heyday it was a lively market town of inns, warehouses and shops. A visitor today walks along restored lanes, looks at boats on the water and eats local snacks.

The countryside around is part of the flat plain between Shandong and Jiangsu, with fields of wheat, maize and sweet potato and small ponds. Roads are straight and the traffic is a mix of lorries and farm vehicles. Late summer thunderstorms can bring flooding, and winter is cold with bitter north winds. Spring blossoms and autumn colours, with clear light and mild air, are the best times.

The nearest town with services is Pizhou, about thirty-four kilometres away with eighty thousand people, and the larger city of Zaozhuang lies just over the border in Shandong. Fuel and food are easy to find along the main roads. Regional food includes spicy chicken soup, flatbread with scallions and Shandong's famous steamed buns. Foreign riders in China face strict rules about licences, plates and guides, so check ahead and prepare the paperwork. It is also wise to bring cash and a translation app, because English is rarely spoken outside the big cities.
t.yangzhou section of huaiyang canal@32.8,:
Gaoyou is a small canal city in central Jiangsu, set between two big lakes, and it has been a staging post on the Grand Canal for over two thousand years. The Gaoyou and Shaobo lakes lie on either side of the waterway, and the old canal embankment runs between them, a long ridge of earth and stone that carried the boats north and south. At this point the Huaiyang section meets the Yangzhou stretch, the part of the canal that ran from the Yangtze north to the Huai river, and it was one of the busiest stretches of the whole system.

The town has its own reputation. Gaoyou is known across China for its salted duck eggs, pickled in brine until the yolk turns into a bright red-orange, oily paste, and a Gaoyou egg is a proud product, served at breakfast with rice porridge. The poet Qin Guan, a Song dynasty writer known for his delicate love poems, was born here, and the town honours him with a memorial. Old streets near the canal keep some of the atmosphere of the past, with tiled roofs and narrow alleys.

The landscape is wet and flat, a country of water. Fields of rice and rapeseed run to the edge of the dykes, carp ponds and lotus pools lie between the villages, and the lakes are full of birds, including egrets, herons and ducks. In spring, the rapeseed blooms in yellow sheets, and in autumn the reeds turn silver. The sky is often soft and hazy, and summers are hot and humid, with typhoon rains in late summer.

The riding is flat, with long straight roads and little change in direction, and surfaces can be rough on village lanes. Visitors who want to ride in China should check the rules on licences and temporary registration well in advance, since requirements are strict and change. Gaoyou has fuel stations, shops and restaurants, and the larger city of Yangzhou, with its gardens and canal views, lies to the south. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, and the best food is local: freshwater fish, steamed buns and the famous eggs.
t.site of caoyun governor s mansion@33.5,1:
Huai'an was a city made by water, and the water was money. Where the Grand Canal met the Huai river, and for centuries the Yellow River as well, the city stood at the most delicate junction on the whole waterway, a knot of channels, locks and dykes that controlled the flow of grain from the south to Beijing. The government posted an official here to supervise it, the Governor-General of Grain Transport, and the site of his headquarters, the Caoyun mansion, preserves the remains of that bureaucracy. It lies in the old Qingjiangpu district, and it belongs to the Grand Canal's UNESCO listing, which came in 2014.

What the governor managed was a vast system. Tens of thousands of boatmen, soldiers and clerks worked to move millions of piculs of tribute grain up the canal each year, and the ships waited in queues at the locks at Qingkou, where the canal crossed the river. Repairs were endless, since the Yellow River silted up the channels and flooded the plain, and the court spent huge sums on dykes. The scale of the effort tells you something about the empire: the capital's survival depended on a single, fragile ditch.

The city has produced famous people. The novelist Wu Cheng'en, who wrote Journey to the West, was born here in the sixteenth century, and Zhou Enlai, the first premier of the People's Republic, was brought up in Huai'an, and his old home is a museum. The local cooking is a branch of the Huaiyang tradition, delicate and sweet, with a reputation for freshwater fish and river eel, served in elaborate banquets of many courses.

The surrounding country is flat, wet farmland, with rice paddies, fish ponds and the huge Hongze Lake to the west. Roads follow the canal and cross it on bridges, with trucks, scooters and agricultural vehicles sharing them, and the air in summer is hot and heavy. Visitors who want to ride in China should check the rules on licences and registration, which are strict. Huai'an is a city of more than half a million people, so fuel, hotels and food are easy, and the canal in the evening, with its lights and its slow barges, is worth a walk. Spring and autumn are the best seasons.
t.accra@5.6,-0.2:
Accra is hot, humid and loud, and it is built on a coast that has seen traders for more than five hundred years. Portuguese, Dutch, Danish, Swedish and British merchants all built forts along this shore, and the city grew around a few of them: Jamestown, the old British quarter with its lighthouse and fishing harbour, and Osu, with the Danish castle that once served as the seat of government. Today Accra is the capital of Ghana, with nearly two million people in the city itself and many more in the sprawl around it.

Independence Arch, near the sea, commemorates the day in 1957 when Ghana became the first sub-Saharan African country to win independence from colonial rule, and Kwame Nkrumah, the leader of the movement, lies in a mausoleum nearby. The city's music, a mix of highlife and hip-hop, spills out of every taxi, and street food is plentiful, from grilled fish to fried plantain and spicy stews of beans.

Riding here demands energy. The traffic is heavy and unpredictable, with minibuses, taxis, lorries and motorcycles all competing for space, and the roads can be potholed. Drive defensively, watch for pedestrians crossing without warning, and avoid the peak hours, when roads grind to a halt. Fuel is easy to find, with stations all around, and food stalls line most main streets. A ride west toward the old forts begins on the coastal highway toward Kasoa, and early morning is the best time to set off, when the air is cooler and the roads are emptier.

The weather is warm all year, with a long rainy season from April to July and a shorter one in autumn. Carry water and wear sun protection. The sea breeze in the late afternoon is a relief, and in the evening the beaches fill with people playing football, selling snacks and watching the waves roll in.
t.forts and castles@5.4,-0.5:
Along the coast west of Accra, a string of white fortresses stands on headlands above the surf. They were built by European traders from the fifteenth century onward, first by the Portuguese, who founded Elmina in 1482 to buy gold, then by the Dutch, the British, the Danes and others, who competed for the trade in gold and, later, enslaved people. The forts and castles of the Gold Coast are now a UNESCO World Heritage site, a sobering reminder of how this coast was shaped.

The checkpoint here lies on the coast near Winneba, a town of around 44,000 people with a lively fishing harbour and a university. The ride heads west from Accra along the main coastal road, passing through Kasoa, where traffic often builds, and then along the sea, with views of palm groves, fishing villages and long beaches. Brightly painted boats are drawn up on the sand, nets are spread out to dry, and the air smells of salt and smoke from the fish ovens.

The riding is hot work, and the road surface varies, with good tarmac in places and potholes in others. Heavy lorries and shared taxis share the road, and speed bumps appear at villages, sometimes without warning, so stay alert. Fuel is available in Winneba and Kasoa, and it is wise to top up before you go further west, as stations can be sparse on long stretches. Carry water, and try to start early.

Further west, at Cape Coast and Elmina, the two largest castles dominate the shore, and guided tours lead through dark dungeons and out onto sunlit ramparts, where cannon still point at the sea. It is a moving and uncomfortable visit, and one that stays with you. Let the sea wind cool you after, and take time to sit with a cold drink, and think about what the walls have seen.
t.ubud@-8.5,115.3:
Ubud is the place where Bali's rice paddies meet its art. Set in the hills at the island's centre, the town grew from a royal village into a centre for painters, dancers and carvers in the 1920s and 1930s, when European artists such as Walter Spies, a German, and Rudolf Bonnet, a Dutchman, settled here and encouraged local painters to explore new styles. The old royal palace, the Puri Saren, still hosts dance performances in the evenings, with gamelan music and elaborate costumes.

The landscape around is a patchwork of terraced rice fields, steep river gorges and jungle. Walking the ridge at Campuhan at dawn, with mist in the valleys and the first light on the coconut palms, is a fine start to the day. The Monkey Forest, a sacred forest sanctuary in the town, is full of long-tailed macaques with a habit of snatching sunglasses. Nearly 30,000 people live in the town itself, and the surrounding villages hold many more.

The riding is a mixture of delight and difficulty. The roads out of Ubud lead north to the highlands, past rice terraces and temples, and the corners are tight, with steep climbs and sudden drops. The surface can be uneven, with potholes and gravel, and traffic is heavy, especially around Ubud itself, where scooters, trucks and tour buses fill the lanes by mid-morning. An early start is a great help. Petrol is sold in stations in the town and, in smaller villages, in bottles from roadside stalls.

Balinese Hinduism shapes every day. Offerings of flowers and rice are placed at doorways and on the pavement, and ceremonies fill the roads with processions in white and gold. Once a year, on Nyepi, the Day of Silence, the whole island shuts down for twenty-four hours, with no traffic, no lights and no travel, so check the date before planning a trip. The dry season, from April to October, is the best time. Food is excellent, with roast duck, suckling pig and fresh fruit everywhere.
t.cultural landscape of bali province the:
Lake Batur lies in the bowl of an ancient volcanic caldera in the highlands of north-central Bali, and from the rim above it the view is unforgettable. The lake is crescent-shaped, with a young black cone, Mount Batur, rising from the caldera floor at about 1,700 metres, still steaming from vents on its flank. The road runs along the crater rim at Penelokan, a name that means the place to look, and on a clear morning the mist lies in the basin like milk in a bowl.

This is one of the heartlands of Bali's remarkable irrigation system, the subak, which UNESCO has listed as a cultural landscape. For a thousand years the farmers of the island have shared water through a network of canals, tunnels and weirs, governed by priests and village councils who treat the water as a gift of the gods. At the centre of it stands the temple of Ulun Danu Batur, where offerings are made to the goddess of the lake, whose waters feed the springs that irrigate the rice terraces far below. The temple was moved up the slope after an eruption in 1926 buried the old village, and local people say the lava stopped at its gate.

The air is cool at this altitude, often damp, and a jacket is welcome. The road from Ubud climbs through Tampaksiring, and the bends tighten as you rise, with views over terraces and forest. Surfaces are generally good on the main road but poor on side lanes, and fog can come down quickly. On the far side of the lake, the village of Trunyan keeps an old practice of leaving its dead beneath a sacred tree, a custom that sets it apart from the rest of Bali.

Fuel is available in the larger villages around the rim, but it is sensible to start with a full tank. Sunrise treks up Mount Batur leave in the dark, and early mornings at the crater are crowded. Visit in the dry season, from May to September, and expect the air to be crisp and clear. Nothing quite prepares you for the sight of the lake in the first light.
t.klamath falls@42.2,-121.8:
Klamath Falls sits on the south end of Upper Klamath Lake, a broad shallow sheet of water that is the largest lake by surface area in Oregon, and the whole town faces it. Tucked in a high basin of the Cascades' eastern flank, at over a thousand metres, the city of twenty-odd thousand has a dry, sunny, big-sky character, more like the high desert than the green coastal Oregon of postcards. The Link River tumbles through town, connecting the lake to the Klamath River, which flows west to the Pacific through a wild, deep canyon.

The region has a rich history. The Klamath and Modoc peoples lived here long before settlers arrived, and the Modoc War of the early 1870s was fought a short distance south, at the lava beds. The basin later became a centre of cattle, timber and irrigated farming, and the town grew around the railway. Today, it is a practical place, home to a technical university that heats its buildings with geothermal water from beneath the town, a quiet quirk that goes back decades. The wetlands and lakes of the basin are important bird habitat, with huge flocks of waterfowl on migration, and in winter bald eagles gather in good numbers.

For a rider, this is the start of the Volcanic Legacy Scenic Byway, a long route linking Crater Lake with Mount Shasta through lava fields, pine forests and old volcanoes. Highway 97 runs north and south through the basin, a wide, fast road with views of the lake and mountains, while Highway 140 climbs west toward Lake of the Woods, a delightful, curving mountain road. Crater Lake, about an hour north, is among the finest sights in the United States, though its rim road closes with snow for much of the year.

Fuel, supermarkets and diners are easy to find in town. Weather here is dry, with hot summer days and chilly nights, and winter brings snow and ice. The best time to ride is late spring to early autumn. In the evening, the sun sets over the lake in a long, orange wash, and pelicans glide low across the water. Pack layers, because nights are cold.
t.roseburg@43.2,-123.3:
Roseburg is the main town of the Umpqua valley in southern Oregon, with around twenty-two thousand people, an old timber economy and a position right where Interstate 5 crosses the South Umpqua River. For many years the city was proud to call itself the Timber Capital of the Nation, and mills, logging trucks and sawdust were everyday companions. The industry has shrunk, but the town still carries a rugged working feel, with a pleasant old downtown, murals, and several breweries.

In 1959 a truck loaded with explosives caught fire and detonated in the centre of town, flattening buildings and killing several people, an event still talked about locally. The area also has wine, with small vineyards on the sunny hills around the valley producing pinot noir and some unusual varieties. Further out, the nearby wildlife park lets you drive past lions, bears and other animals.

For riders, Roseburg is the doorway to the Umpqua country. Highway 138, the North Umpqua Highway, heads east up the river toward Crater Lake, following a river famous for fly fishing and steelhead. The road is gently winding at first, through green forested canyons, and then steepens, with long curves, fast sweeping sections and occasional tight corners. Along the way a string of waterfalls, including the impressive Toketee and Watson falls, make good short walks from the road.

The Cascade Range rises above, and Crater Lake itself, the deep blue lake formed in the crater of a collapsed volcano, sits at the end of the route. It is one of the deepest lakes in the United States, famously clear and strikingly blue. The high road to the rim is usually blocked by snow for much of the year, normally from late autumn into early summer, so check the park's seasonal information before setting off.

Roseburg has fuel at every corner, supermarkets and plenty of ordinary American diners. After the town there are long stretches with little, so top up before leaving. The best months are late June to September, though summer afternoons can be hot in the valley and wildfire smoke sometimes drifts through late in the season. Mornings are cool and clear.
t.plateau de carnac bassin du gouyanzeur@4:
Carnac is the greatest concentration of standing stones in the world, and the sheer number is hard to believe until you see it. More than three thousand granite blocks, set in long, straight rows, march across the heathland north of the town, in alignments called Ménec, Kermario and Kerlescan. They were raised by Neolithic people between about 4500 and 3300 BC, long before Stonehenge or the pyramids, and nobody knows exactly why. Theories range from calendars and tombs to ritual processions, and the stones themselves, grey, lichened and leaning, stay silent. The coastal landscape of Morbihan is now recognised on UNESCO's World Heritage list.

Local legend has its own explanation: the saint Cornély, chased by Roman soldiers, turned them to stone to save himself, and the rows are the army still standing in file. The Saint-Michel tumulus, a great mound at the edge of the town, covers a Neolithic burial chamber and has a small chapel on top, with a long view of the bay and the rows of stones. The country around is a low, windswept plateau of gorse, heather and pines, with the Atlantic only a few kilometres away, and the light is often soft and silvery.

Riding here is easy and pleasant. The roads across the plateau are mostly flat and straight, with gentle bends through villages of low granite houses, and the coast roads run beside beaches and oyster beds. Sea wind can be strong and cold, even in summer, and weather arrives quickly off the Atlantic, so pack a waterproof layer. Plouharnel, Carnac and Auray are all within easy reach, and Auray, a town of twelve thousand people with a pretty old harbour at Saint-Goustan, is the best place for fuel and a longer lunch, though Carnac has stations and bakeries as well.

Try to walk in the stones early, before the coaches arrive. The alignments are best seen in the low, golden light of morning or evening, and in the busy season, access to some stretches is limited to protect the ground, with fenced areas and viewing paths. Buy salted-butter caramels in town as a souvenir, and watch the tide go out across the bay.
t.rennes@48.1,-1.7:
Rennes is the capital of Brittany, a handsome, youthful city of two hundred thousand people on the river Vilaine, with a large student population and a lively street life. The old quarter has a surprising number of half-timbered houses from the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, leaning at crazy angles, which survived a great fire in 1720 that destroyed much of the rest of the town. After that disaster, the centre was rebuilt in an orderly grid of stone, and the contrast between the two styles is part of the city's charm.

t.bali@-8.4,115.2:

Temples are everywhere, with carved stone gates and tall tiered roofs, and ceremonies bring processions of women carrying towers of fruit on their heads. A few kilometres south, at Mengwi, the royal water temple of Taman Ayun sits in a moat of lotus ponds, one of the most elegant temples on the island.

The quiet back lanes between villages are narrow, with sharp bends, patches of gravel, dogs, chickens and ceremonies blocking the road, and traffic moves slowly and politely. Warung serve nasi campur and fresh fruit for little money, and a coconut by the road is the cheapest cold drink. Aim to ride early, before the heat and traffic build, and finish with a swim.
t.lake batur@-8.3,115.4:
Lake Batur fills part of an enormous volcanic caldera in north-east Bali, and the first view of it, from the rim at Penelokan, is one of the island's best. The word Penelokan means a place to look, and the sight justifies it: a huge crescent of dark water about a thousand metres up, with the active cone of Mount Batur rising from the crater floor, and beyond it the bigger bulk of Mount Abang. A bigger sibling, Mount Agung, stands to the east, and at over three thousand metres it is the island's highest and most sacred peak. Batur itself last erupted in the early 2000s, and lava flows from earlier eruptions are still visible as black fields on the slopes.

The temple of Pura Ulun Danu Batur, on the rim, honours the goddess of the lake, who is believed to provide water for the whole island's rice fields, and is among the most important on Bali. On the far shore, the village of Trunyan has an unusual way of treating its dead, and below the rim, at Toya Bungkah, hot springs bubble up for bathing. The surface is mostly good, though trucks carrying vegetables and tour minibuses crowd the narrow sections, and sellers at the viewpoints can be persistent.

The nearest big towns are some distance away, Bedugul about thirty kilometres to the west and Klungkung a little further south, and the villages on the rim have little in the way of services, so begin with a full tank. Roadside warung and a few lakeside restaurants offer fried fish from the lake, corn, noodles and strong coffee. Mist, rain and slippery roads are common in the wet season, from November to March, and the dry months bring clearer views. Keep a layer ready for the evening descent.
t.gold hill@42.4,-123.0:
Gold Hill lives up to its name in a modest way. Locals fish for salmon and steelhead in the Rogue, and rafting companies run the stretches of river below.

The byway uses a combination of state highways, and the final approach through the valley is flatter, with orchards, vineyards and hay fields on the valley floor.

Just across the river, the two flat-topped Table Rocks rise above the valley, a pair of basalt mesas sacred to the Takelma people who lived here before settlers came. In 1853 a treaty was signed at the foot of one of them, and violence in the following years, the Rogue River Wars, ended with the forced removal of Native people to reservations on the coast. Hiking trails lead to the top of the Table Rocks, and the wildflowers in spring are remarkable.

Wine is a feature of this valley, with a number of vineyards and tasting rooms, though riders will want to be careful with that. Spring and early autumn are the best seasons, with clear air and mild days, while summer afternoons can reach well into the thirties, and winter brings fog and frost.

The mountain, a huge plug-dome volcano at the southern end of the Cascade Range, rises to 10,457 feet above a landscape of scorched slopes, steaming vents, boiling mud pots and lakes that sit in craters. In May 1915 an explosion sent a column of ash high into the sky and a mudflow swept down the valley, leaving the sparse, ghostly stretch known as the Devastated Area. Today the area is a national park, with forest and meadow creeping back across the lava.

The park road is thirty miles of mountain riding, with long climbs, tight switchbacks and views across lakes and ridges. It tops out at about 8,500 feet at the highest point, with Lassen Peak looming on one side, and the air is thin and cool even in midsummer. The road is generally well surfaced but narrow in places, with broken edges where frost has worked on it. Snow closes it for much of the year, normally from November to about June, and in some years the final stretch opens only in July, so check with the park before riding.

The smell of sulphur is strong, and visitors should keep to the boardwalks. Manzanita Lake, near the north entrance, has a classic view of Lassen Peak mirrored in the water, best in the stillness of early morning.

t.sisters oregon@44.3,-121.5:

t.mckenzie pass@44.3,-121.8:
McKenzie Pass has a split personality. At 5,325 feet, about 1,623 metres, the pass is a high, windy, exposed place, with the snowy peaks of the Three Sisters rising above the lava and Mount Washington, a spire of eroded volcanic rock, standing alone to the north.

t.sisters@44.3,-121.5:
Sisters sits on the dry east side of the Oregon Cascades, at about 3,200 feet, in a patch of ponderosa pine and sagebrush where the forest gives way to high desert. t.denpasar@-8.6,115.2:
Denpasar is the capital of Bali and a city that most visitors drive around rather than into, which is a shame because it is the part of the island that works for the Balinese rather than for tourists. It is crowded, noisy and full of scooters, with markets selling offerings, spices and fabrics, and temples tucked between shops. Puputan Square, the central park, commemorates the day in 1906 when the Balinese court, facing Dutch troops, walked out in ceremonial dress and chose death over surrender, an event known as the puputan. Every morning, women set out small woven trays of flowers and rice on pavements, shrines and the dashboards of cars, and every few days a procession blocks the road for an hour with music, parasols and offerings. t.mataram@-8.6,116.1:
Mataram is the capital of Lombok, the island east of Bali across a deep and swift strait, and it is a much quieter and more traditional place than its famous neighbour. Its crater holds a lake and a smaller cone, and trekkers set out from villages on its flanks to climb it. Visible from almost everywhere, it gives the island its character. Sasak villages with thatched roofs and woven bamboo walls can be visited in the countryside, and weaving is a living craft.

From Mataram, the road runs north along the coast through Senggigi, where the sea is a deep turquoise, then loops inland on mountain roads through forests and past waterfalls. In the wet season, from November to March, rain can be heavy.

t.tegallalang@-8.4,115.3:

They are part of a system called subak, an ancient method of irrigation and communal water management that dates back about a thousand years, and which is run by farmers' associations according to the Balinese Hindu philosophy of harmony between people, nature and the gods. UNESCO listed the subak landscape as a World Heritage Site in 2012, and the fields here are a living example.

The rice cycle takes about four months, from flooded green seedlings to golden grain, so the colour varies through the year. In recent years, cafés and swings have appeared along the ridge, charging entry for photographs, and the site is often busy with visitors. Even so, farmers still plant and harvest by hand, and small offerings of flowers and incense are placed at the corners of the fields and at the little water temples, thanking the goddess of rice.

Scooters are the main form of transport, and the roads are narrow, busy and chaotic, with trucks, dogs, chickens, ceremonial processions and sudden turns. Traffic drives on the left, and the pace is slow in villages. The road from Ubud to Tegallalang is crowded with tour vans and bikes, so patience is essential. Tegallalang itself is famous for wood carving and stone sculptures, and the roadside is lined with workshops selling furniture, masks and statues. Offerings in small palm-leaf trays, called canang sari, are laid on the road each morning, and riders are expected to avoid them where possible.

Cafés near the terraces serve coffee, fruit juices and nasi goreng, with views over the fields. Carry small cash for entrance donations and parking.
t.kintamani@-8.2,115.4:
Kintamani sits on the rim of an enormous volcanic caldera, at around fifteen hundred metres, and the air is noticeably cooler than on the coast. The caldera is about ten kilometres across, a vast bowl formed by massive eruptions in prehistoric times, and inside it stand the cone of Mount Batur, still active, and the crescent-shaped Lake Batur, dark blue under the cliffs. The Balinese Hindu villages of the region keep ancient traditions, and the nearby village of Trunyan, on the lake, is known for its unusual burial customs, in which the dead are laid out under a tree rather than cremated. Kintamani is also home to temples, such as Pura Ulun Danu Batur, dedicated to the goddess of the lake and the source of water for much of Bali's irrigation.

Mist and cloud are common in the afternoon, so the morning is the best time to enjoy the view. The dry season, from April to October, is the most reliable. A jacket is sensible, because the temperature can fall to around fifteen degrees in the early morning.

Fuel stations are available in Kintamani and in the larger towns on the route. Ubud, about thirty kilometres away, is the largest centre for services. Carry cash, and allow plenty of time, since distances on Bali take longer than expected.
t.mount batur viewpoint@-8.3,115.4:
Mount Batur is a volcano with a short temper. It rises to 1,717 metres from the floor of a vast caldera, beside the crescent of Lake Batur, and it has erupted many times in recorded history, leaving black fields of cooled lava on its flanks. Smoke and steam still seep from vents near the summit, and the ground in places is warm to the touch. The volcano is a place of deep significance to the Balinese, who believe that its spirit controls the water that feeds the island's rice terraces, and offerings are made to the lake goddess at the temple on the shore.

The viewpoints along the caldera rim give the best view of the whole scene: the cone in the foreground, the dark lake beyond, and in the distance, the larger peak of Mount Abang on the opposite rim. On a clear day, you can see Mount Agung, Bali's highest mountain at 3,031 metres, rising to the east. Many visitors climb Batur before dawn, setting out at two or three in the morning with a guide and a torch, to reach the summit for sunrise, with the clouds spread out below. Mist, drizzle and low cloud are frequent, and the view can disappear in minutes, so check the weather. The road into the caldera floor, from Penelokan, drops steeply in a series of hairpins to the lake shore, and it is a good ride, though the surface is rough in places.

t.besakih@-8.4,115.5:
Besakih is the Mother Temple of Bali, the largest and holiest Hindu temple on the island, and it sits high on the southern slope of Mount Agung, the great volcano that dominates the east. The oldest parts may date back many centuries, and the complex is still in daily use for ceremonies.

The lava and ash flows came close to Besakih, and the story goes that the flow of lava stopped just short of the temple, which the Balinese regarded as a miracle and a sign of the temple's sacred protection. Whatever the explanation, the temple survived, and it remains central to Balinese religious life. The best time to visit is early morning, when the mountain is clear and the temperature is cool, and clouds usually cover the summit by midday. The dry season is more reliable, and rain can make the road slippery.

t.mount bachelor@44.0,-121.7:

t.elk lake@44.0,-121.8:
