t.lava lake@43.9,-121.8:
The name tells you most of it. Lava Lake exists because a flow of molten rock once dammed the valley, trapping the spring water and snowmelt that seeped through the volcanic ground. It sits at about forty-eight hundred feet on the Cascade Lakes Scenic Byway, ringed by pine forest, with the Three Sisters visible on a clear day. Right beside it is Little Lava Lake, which is the headwaters of the Deschutes River, one of the best-known rivers in Oregon, and a quiet spring that gives birth to a major waterway.

The ground here is porous. Rain and snow sink into the lava rock and emerge as springs, which is why the Deschutes starts as such a steady, cold stream rather than a flashy mountain torrent. The surrounding forest is lodgepole and ponderosa pine, and in the meadows near the edges you may see elk and deer. Birds are easy to watch, from ospreys fishing in the lake to waterfowl on the shallows, and the quiet is broken mostly by wind and the occasional boat.

The byway here is a gentle, well-surfaced road, without the intensity of the section near Mount Bachelor. The curves are easy, the gradients mild, and the traffic usually light. It is a good place to relax on a bike, enjoy the mountain air, and take your time. The season is short: heavy snow closes the high section of the byway in winter, and ice can linger into May. Summer afternoons can bring thunderstorms, and the temperatures drop quickly after dark even in August.

Bend, a good thirty-odd kilometres to the east, has the stations, restaurants, and shops, and Sunriver and Three Rivers are smaller settlements closer by. Bring snacks and water, and keep a spare layer in the pannier. Mosquitoes in early summer can be fierce, and the lake is cold enough to discourage all but the hardiest swimmers. The best time of day is early morning, when the lake is calm and the reflections are sharp.
t.sparks lake@43.9,-121.7:
Sparks Lake is a photographer's lake, and the photographers know it. It is a shallow, irregular sheet of water on the Cascade Lakes Scenic Byway, with dead trees standing in the shallows and black lava rock along the shore, and at the far end rise the Three Sisters and Broken Top. At dawn, when the water is still and the light is soft, the whole range appears in the water with a clarity that almost looks staged. People arrive before sunrise with tripods and thermoses, and the lake is quiet and cold.

The lake exists thanks to a lava flow that dammed the valley, much like its neighbours. Soda Creek, which feeds it, flows through a landscape of volcanic rock that is among the youngest in the Cascades, and the lake is shallow enough that it shrinks in late summer. Some of the dead trees in the water are the result of old changes in level. Birdlife is rich, with ducks, herons, and the occasional osprey, and in the evening it is not unusual to hear coyotes.

The ride along this stretch is among the best of the byway. The road winds through forest and lava fields, with gentle curves, short climbs, and views that change with every bend. The surface is generally smooth, and the traffic is light outside the weekends. A short gravel road leads to the lake itself, which may be loose and dusty in places, so take care on a heavy bike. Snow closes the byway for much of the winter, and mud and ice are possible in late spring.

Bend is the place to fill up and eat, and it lies about fifty kilometres east, with Sunriver and Three Rivers somewhat closer. Carry water, and wear sun protection, since the air at this altitude is thin and the sun is strong. The best time of day is early morning for the reflections and again at dusk, when the shadows lengthen and the lava shows black against the pale grass. In late summer the water is low, and in autumn the colours in the nearby meadows are rich.
t.borzya@50.4,116.5:
Borzya is a railway and steppe town of some thirty thousand people in the far southeast of Zabaykalsky Krai, close to both the Mongolian and Chinese borders. The country around it is Dauria, a high, dry grassland that stretches across the corner where Russia, Mongolia and China meet, and the town stands on the Borzya River with a long, low skyline of Soviet housing blocks, grain silos and rail yards. It is a working place, and its role has always been about moving things: grain, coal, livestock and the occasional rider with dust on his visor.

For a motorcyclist it is an honest, useful stop. Fuel is easy to find, there are shops and cafes, and a handful of places to sleep. Do not expect polish; do expect a plate of meat, rice and salad, a pot of black tea and a friendly question about where you are headed. Chita is a long way behind, and the Dauria reserve lies further south and east, so use the town to top up, buy water and food for the steppe, and check your bike. Oil and tyres are not always easy to find in smaller villages.

The ride to Borzya crosses an enormous, almost treeless plain. The road is straight for kilometres, with long rolling rises that reveal more of the same, and wind is the dominant feature of the riding. A headwind can eat your fuel and your patience, and a crosswind can push a loaded bike around. Summer days are hot, with high skies and flickering mirages, and storms build quickly in the afternoon. Spring and autumn bring cold, dust and bare brown hills, and the best light is in the early morning and late evening, when the steppe turns amber.

History has left strange marks here. In the chaos after 1917 the baron Roman von Ungern-Sternberg operated in Dauria, and local memory still connects him to the area around the nearby railway station. The steppe is also a corridor for migrating birds and herds of Mongolian gazelle, and in some seasons you can spot cranes and raptors from the road. It is a landscape that rewards slow looking, with the horizon always a little farther than it seems.
t.la citadelle et le fort pate et medoc de:
The Gironde estuary is wide enough here to feel like an inland sea, and Vauban saw it as the gateway to Bordeaux that needed a lock. His answer, at the end of the seventeenth century, was a triangle of fortifications: the citadel at Blaye on the right bank, Fort Médoc on the left bank at Cussac, and between them Fort Paté, a squat stone tower built on an island in the middle of the river. Together they could cross their fire over the shipping channel, and today they share a place on the UNESCO list of Vauban's works. The citadel of Blaye is the most impressive of the three, a fortified town in its own right, with ramparts, gates and old barracks set high on a bluff above the water.

Walking the walls is free, and the views across the estuary are wide and atmospheric, especially in the evening light, when the water turns silver and the Médoc shore becomes a low line on the horizon. Blaye's history goes further back than Vauban. The troubadour Jaufré Rudel was a lord of Blaye in the twelfth century, famous for his songs of distant love, and medieval legend held that Roland, the hero of the Chanson de Roland, was buried here. Later, the Duchess of Berry was held prisoner in the citadel in the 1830s after a failed royalist uprising.

The riding around Blaye is gentle and pleasant rather than dramatic. The Côtes de Blaye vineyards roll over low hills, with quiet country roads linking villages, chateaux and churches. The estuary road towards Bourg is a nice ride, with the river on one side and limestone cliffs on the other, some of them pocked with cave dwellings. Wind can be a factor, coming in off the Atlantic and funnelling up the estuary.

A small car ferry crosses the estuary from Blaye to Lamarque, a short crossing that drops you in the heart of the Médoc wine country near Fort Médoc and the great chateaux of Margaux and Pauillac. Blaye has fuel, shops and restaurants, and the town's market and its cafes make a good lunch stop. Try the local wines, of course, and if you see lamprey on a menu, that is the estuary speciality, cooked slowly in red wine.
t.sword beach@49.3,-0.3:
On the morning of 6 June 1944 this long, flat stretch of sand between Ouistreham and Lion-sur-Mer was the easternmost of the five Allied landing beaches in Normandy. British troops of the 3rd Infantry Division came ashore here, supported by commandos, including a small unit of French commandos under Philippe Kieffer, who fought their way into Ouistreham. The beach linked up with the airborne forces who had taken the bridges over the Orne and the Caen canal during the night, among them the famous Pegasus Bridge at Bénouville, a few kilometres inland. Lord Lovat's commandos marched to relieve the paratroopers there, led, according to the well-known story, by piper Bill Millin playing on the beach under fire.

Today the beach is a holiday shore again, lined with villas, beach huts and promenades, and it takes a little imagination to picture the scene of that morning. Memorials and plaques are scattered along the seafront in Hermanville, Colleville-Montgomery and Ouistreham, and the museum of the Atlantic Wall in Ouistreham is housed in a former German concrete fire-control tower. Pegasus Bridge, with the original bridge preserved in the memorial museum, is worth the short ride inland.

The riding here is easy, with flat roads following the coast and running inland through farmland and small villages. The coast road links all the landing beaches, from Sword through Juno and Gold to Omaha and Utah further west, and many riders make a day or two of it, stopping at the cemeteries, museums and memorials along the way. Traffic can be heavy in summer and around the anniversaries, especially near the main sites. The weather is changeable, with wind and rain common, so pack accordingly.

Ouistreham, a town of about nine thousand people, has all the services you could need, as well as a ferry port with crossings to Portsmouth, which makes it a natural starting or finishing point for riders coming from Britain. The town has a good choice of restaurants and seafood, and the market is lively. Inland, Caen offers a larger city with its castle and abbeys, built by William the Conqueror, a reminder that the links between Normandy and England are far older than the war.
t.gold beach@49.3,-0.6:
On the morning of 6 June 1944 the British 50th Northumbrian Division came ashore along this low, sandy coast between La Rivière and Arromanches, and almost everything you see from the dunes at Ver-sur-Mer is shaped by that day. Gold Beach was the middle of the five Allied landing zones, with Juno to the east and Omaha to the west, and it is the quietest of them to ride today: a string of small seaside villages, wide flat sands at low tide and a coast road that ambles rather than races.

Ver-sur-Mer is where the British Normandy Memorial now stands on the slope above the shore, a long colonnade carrying the names of the men under British command who died in the campaign. It is a sobering, beautifully made place, and the view from it over the beach makes the geography of the landing obvious in a way no map does. Nearby, Company Sergeant Major Stanley Hollis of the Green Howards won the only Victoria Cross awarded for actions on D-Day itself. A few kilometres west, the concrete caissons of the Mulberry harbour still sit in the sea off Arromanches like broken teeth, and the German battery at Longues-sur-Mer keeps its guns pointed at the Channel.

The riding here is gentle. The D514 follows the coast through Courseulles, Ver and Asnelles, with roundabouts, speed bumps and plenty of summer traffic, while the lanes inland towards Creully run between open wheat fields and stone farm villages with high walls. Wind off the Channel is a constant companion and can push a light bike around on the exposed stretches. Early morning or a late September evening is the time to come, when the coach parties have gone and the light goes soft and silver over the sand.

For anything more than a coffee, Bayeux is the natural base, thirteen kilometres inland, with fuel, supermarkets and the tapestry that tells an earlier cross-Channel invasion in the other direction. Courseulles-sur-Mer has fuel too, plus oyster stalls on the harbour and plenty of cafés. Ver itself is small, but there is usually somewhere open in season for a crêpe and a cider, which feels like the right way to sit for a while and look at the water.
t.pointe du hoc@49.4,-1.0:
Pointe du Hoc is a headland of grey cliffs, about thirty metres high, between Omaha and Utah beaches on the Normandy coast, and it is one of the most moving places on the whole D-Day shore. On the morning of 6 June 1944, some two hundred and twenty-five US Army Rangers under Lieutenant Colonel James Rudder came in by landing craft, fired grappling hooks and rope ladders up the cliff, and climbed under fire to take a German battery thought to threaten both beaches. They found the guns had been moved inland, tracked them down and disabled them, then held the position for two days against counterattacks. Fewer than a hundred were still able to fight when they were relieved.

What makes the site so powerful is that it has been left almost as the battle left it. The ground is cratered like the moon by the naval bombardment, the concrete casemates are broken and tilted, and you can walk among them on paths to the observation post at the tip, with the Channel wind in your face. A granite pylon stands on the bunker at the point as a memorial. The site is cared for by the American Battle Monuments Commission and there is a small visitor centre.

The riding along this coast is gentle and atmospheric rather than technical. The D514 follows the shoreline through Grandcamp-Maisy, Vierville and Port-en-Bessin, with hedged lanes, stone farmhouses and views of the sea, and almost every village has its plaque, its museum or its preserved tank. Traffic builds heavily around the early June anniversaries, when the area fills with veterans' groups, reenactors and old jeeps. The rest of the summer is busy too; shoulder seasons are calmer, though the wind can be bitter.

Grandcamp-Maisy, three kilometres away, is a fishing port with cafes and seafood; scallops are its pride in season. For fuel and a larger supermarket, Isigny-sur-Mer, known for its butter, cream and caramels, or Carentan to the west are the reliable choices. Normandy cider and Calvados are everywhere. Bring a layer even in summer: the headland is fully exposed and weather can blow in fast from the Atlantic.
t.les tours observatoires de tatihou et de:
On the eastern shore of the Cotentin peninsula, in Normandy, the little port of Saint-Vaast-la-Hougue looks out at a low island called Tatihou, and on the island and on the headland of La Hougue stand two stout stone towers designed by Vauban, the military engineer of Louis XIV. They belong to the group of Vauban fortifications that UNESCO inscribed in 2008, and they are among the least known of the twelve sites.

The towers were built in the 1690s after a defeat. In May 1692 the French fleet, sent to cover an invasion of England, was beaten off Cap Barfleur by the combined English and Dutch fleets, and the damaged French ships took refuge in the bay of La Hougue, where they were attacked and burned. Vauban came in person soon afterwards and designed a new defence, a pair of strong towers on either side of the bay, tall cylinders of granite with thick vaults to carry cannon. Tatihou can be reached on foot at low tide, or by a small amphibious vehicle that crosses the sand, and it also has a maritime museum and a bird sanctuary. Check the tide times before you go.

The countryside around is gentle and green, with stone farms, apple orchards and hedged fields, and the coast roads between Barfleur, Saint-Vaast and Quettehou are narrow and scenic, with only occasional traffic in the shoulder season. The wind from the Channel is strong, and rain showers pass quickly. In July and August the roads fill with holidaymakers. Utah Beach, one of the landing beaches of June 1944, lies about twenty-five kilometres to the south-west, with a museum and a long, flat shore.

Saint-Vaast is known for its oysters, farmed in the bay, and for mussels, and the quay is lined with restaurants that serve them with white wine and bread. The village has two thousand people and a few fuel stops, but Valognes, nineteen kilometres inland, has a larger choice and is a handsome town with fine eighteenth-century houses, once called the Versailles of Normandy. Pick a day in late spring or early autumn, when the light is soft and the crowds are small, and bring a waterproof jacket.
t.subak landscape of pekerisan watershed@-:
Bali's rice terraces look natural from a distance, but they are in fact a machine, an old and delicate piece of social engineering that shares water among thousands of farmers. The Pakerisan river runs south from the volcanic highlands near Tampaksiring, and along its length the fields, canals and temples form a landscape that UNESCO listed in 2012 as part of the cultural landscape of Bali, built on the subak system. Ubud, a sizeable town of twenty-eight thousand people, is about ten kilometres to the south-west.

A subak is a cooperative of farmers who share a water supply, and each one has a temple where the priests make offerings to the goddess of rice and the water. They have managed water this way for around a thousand years, and the philosophy behind it, called Tri Hita Karana, speaks of harmony between people, nature and the spirits. The watershed also contains Gunung Kawi, a royal monument from the eleventh century, with shrines carved into the rock face of a river gorge, reached by a long flight of steps down to the water. It is shady, cool and quiet, with the sound of the river and the smell of incense, and the walk back up is steeper than it looks.

The riding here is a matter of patience. The roads between Ubud, Tampaksiring and Klungkung are narrow, busy with scooters, trucks and tourist buses, and flanked by walls and carved stone gates, with potholes, dogs and offerings left on the tarmac. It is not a place for speed, but for slow, observant riding, through villages where roosters crow and shrines stand at every corner. The best light comes in the early morning, before the haze rises and the traffic builds. The dry season, from April to October, is the more comfortable time, while the rains from November to March bring brilliant green terraces and sudden downpours.

Fuel is sold from roadside stalls and at proper stations, and it is easy to find in Ubud and Klungkung. For food, look for a warung selling nasi campur, a plate of rice with small servings of meat, vegetables and sambal, or babi guling, roast suckling pig, which Ubud is famous for. Respect the temples by wearing a sarong and sash when you enter, and never step over an offering on the ground.
t.supreme water temple pura ulun danu batu:
The temple stands on the rim of a caldera, and the caldera is vast. Mount Batur, in the north-east of Bali, sits inside a ring of cliffs some ten kilometres across, left by two huge eruptions tens of thousands of years ago, and in the bowl lies Lake Batur, a crescent of dark water. Pura Ulun Danu Batur is the second most important temple on the island, dedicated to Dewi Danu, the goddess of the lake, whose waters feed the springs and irrigation canals that run down the mountains and water the rice fields of the south. For Balinese farmers, this is where the water comes from, and offerings are made here to keep it flowing.

The temple has a violent history. In 1926 Mount Batur erupted and buried the old village of Batur, and the people believed that the lava stopped at the gate of the temple, leaving it untouched. Afterwards the villagers moved up to the rim and rebuilt the temple there, in a complex of gates, shrines and multi-roofed towers called merus, each with eleven roofs for the lake goddess. UNESCO listed the temple and the whole subak system of rice terraces in 2012 as a cultural landscape. The subak is a farmers' cooperative that shares water by religious calendar and consensus, an arrangement older than any government.

Kintamani, the village on the rim, is cool, often misty, and known for its views over the volcano and lake. The smell of woodsmoke and clove cigarettes drifts on the air, and the coffee is good. Dress properly for the temple, with a sarong and sash, available to hire or borrow at the gate, and expect to pay a small donation.

Riding here means mountain roads. From Ubud the road climbs through villages and forests to the rim with a long series of bends, and traffic can be heavy with tour buses and scooters. Surfaces vary, and rain can come suddenly in the afternoon. Mornings are clearest. Fuel is available in Kintamani and the larger villages along the road, and many small shops sell fuel in bottles. The dry season, from May to September, is the best time.
t.hongcun@30.0,118.0:
From above, Hongcun is said to look like an ox, and the people who built it in the Southern Song and later planned it that way on purpose. A stream, channelled through the village, makes the ox's intestines, two small bridges are the legs, a moon-shaped pond at the centre is its stomach and the hills around are its body, and a pair of ancient trees at the entrance are the horns. It is an engineer's dream as well as a feng shui chart, because the water channels run through the lanes to every house, bringing fresh water for washing and putting out fires, and the Moon Pond is a reflecting pool that mirrors the white walls and curved gables.

The families of Hongcun, mostly named Wang, were merchants who traded salt and tea, and their wealth shows in the mansions of the Ming and Qing periods, with fine carved wood, stone and brick. The Chengzhi Hall, a merchant house with painted beams and a rich interior, is one of the best. With Xidi, the village is listed by UNESCO as part of the Ancient Villages of Southern Anhui. The village also appeared in the film Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon, which brought attention and tourists.

What to expect on arrival is a ticket gate, a car park, and then a wall of photographers at dawn, because the reflections in the pond at first light are the classic shot. Painting students sit at easels around the water, and in autumn the light is soft and the hills fade into blue. The morning mist is common from spring to autumn, and rain is frequent, so the stone paths are slick.

No town is listed nearby in the data, but the area is in Yi county, and the larger centres are the town of Yixian and the city of Huangshan. As with the rest of China, foreign visitors who want to ride must deal with Chinese licensing and registration rules, which in practice limits most of them to hired transport. Plan fuel and meals in Huangshan, bring cash for small stalls, and try the local bamboo-shoot dishes and the hairy tofu, which has a fuzz of white mould and is cooked with a bit of oil and spices. Visit early or late to avoid the groups from tour buses, and remember that it is a living village, so be careful with doors and private courtyards.
t.subak landscape of catur angga batukaru@:
Water is the organising principle of Bali, and the subak is how people organise water. A subak is a farmers' cooperative that manages irrigation for a group of rice fields, with its own rules, its own officials and its own temple, and the system has been working for roughly a thousand years. UNESCO listed the Subak Landscape in 2012, with the temple of Pura Luhur Batukaru on the slopes of Mount Batukaru, the terraced fields around Jatiluwih and the lake temple on Lake Batur among its elements. The philosophy behind it is called Tri Hita Karana, harmony among people, nature and the divine.

Mount Batukaru, at about 2,276 metres, is the second highest peak in Bali, and its forested slopes catch the rain that feeds the rivers and canals below. Pura Luhur Batukaru, set in a damp, mossy forest at the foot of the mountain, is one of the island's most important temples, and a quiet, rather mysterious place with tiered shrines under tall trees. The rice terraces below, in the area of Jatiluwih, step down the hillside in great curving contours, and you can watch farmers tending the paddies, with the sea faint in the distance.

Local rice varieties, including a red one, are grown here, and cooperation among farmers decides when to plant and when to release water. The cycle of planting and harvest is tied to religious ceremonies, and offerings of flowers and rice are left at small shrines beside the fields. It is a landscape that is as much cultural as natural.

Riding in Bali needs a few precautions. Traffic is on the left, roads are narrow and often crowded with scooters, trucks and dogs, and the surface can be broken, wet or covered in leaves. In the mountains the weather changes quickly, with mist and heavy rain, especially in the wet season from roughly November to March. You will need a valid licence that covers a motorcycle and, for foreigners, usually an international permit. Dawn is the best time for the terraces, with soft light and cool air.

Munduk, ten kilometres north, is the nearest sizeable village and has fuel in small roadside stalls and a few cafés. Fill up in the larger towns when you can.
t.area of high dam at the mouth of the val:
Five thousand years ago, on a plain south of Lake Tai, a society built a city with walls, canals, palaces and an advanced water-control system, and then it vanished. Liangzhu, in Zhejiang province not far from Hangzhou, came to light only in the 1930s, and the full extent of its remains was revealed in the early twenty-first century. UNESCO added the Archaeological Ruins of Liangzhu City to its list in 2019, recognising an early regional state in the lower Yangtze valley.

The area of the high dam at the mouth of the valley is one of the key features. Archaeologists found a system of dams, dikes and reservoirs in the hills to the north-west of the city, built around 3000 BC to control floods and store water, and it is among the oldest large-scale hydraulic works known in the world. The earth and straw construction, the scale and the organisation show a sophisticated society with a labour force and planning to match.

The Liangzhu people are best known for their jade. They carved cong, square tubes with circular holes, and bi, flat discs, often with intricate patterns of a masked face, and these objects were buried with the elite. Skilled workers produced them from hard stone with simple tools, and the designs hint at a shared belief system.

The setting is gentle: low green hills, bamboo groves, tea fields and reservoirs, with the city of Hangzhou and its famous West Lake not far to the east. In spring, mist and blossom give the landscape a soft look, and in autumn the air is clear and cool. Summers are hot, humid and often wet.

Honestly, riding here is complicated for foreign visitors. China restricts foreign-registered motorcycles, and most people explore the area by train, bus or taxi from Hangzhou, which is easy and quick. The roads around are good, but local licensing rules apply. Deqing, a town of nearly ninety thousand people about fifteen kilometres away, offers fuel, food and hotels. The museum at Liangzhu is well worth the time, with displays of jade, pottery and models of the city, and there is a park around the main excavation site.
t.si county section of tongji canal@33.5,1:
The Grand Canal of China is the longest artificial waterway in the world, a chain of channels linking Beijing in the north with Hangzhou in the south, and the section through Si County in northern Anhui is part of its oldest and most important layer. The Tongji Canal, built in the early seventh century under the Sui dynasty, linked the Yellow River with the Huai and eventually the Yangtze, and made it possible to move grain and troops from the rich south to the capital. Hundreds of thousands of labourers are said to have dug it, and the project was so costly that it contributed to the collapse of the dynasty.

The Si County stretch has been excavated by archaeologists, who found the remains of the old channel, a lock, embankments and traces of a port town, and it was part of the group that UNESCO inscribed in 2014 as the Grand Canal. What you see on the ground is quiet and modest: a wide, shallow depression running across flat farmland, and perhaps a stretch of water with reeds and willows. That modesty is the point, because the real importance lies in what it made possible.

The land is the great northern plain, flat, fertile and densely cultivated, with wheat in winter and maize in summer, villages of brick houses, and rows of poplars along the roads. The sky is wide and often hazy, and the climate has hot, humid summers and cold, dry winters. Spring and autumn are the most pleasant seasons.

A note on getting here. Riding in China is tightly controlled, and foreign riders face licensing and registration hurdles that make independent touring difficult, so most visitors come by car or train and take a taxi from the county town. The roads in the area are flat, straight and busy with trucks, with expressways and local roads in good condition. The coordinates are far from any large town, with Guiren the nearest listed settlement, about thirty kilometres away, and fuel and food are available there and in the county seat. It is a place for those who are interested in how a country was built, rather than for scenery.
t.crater lake@42.9,-122.1:
Crater Lake does not look real the first time you see it. The water is a deep, saturated blue, almost unnaturally pure, and it fills a bowl nearly ten kilometres across, with steep walls rising some six hundred metres above the surface. It formed about 7,700 years ago, when the volcano Mount Mazama erupted so violently that it emptied its magma chamber and collapsed in on itself. Rain and snow slowly filled the caldera, and with no rivers flowing in or out, the water stayed exceptionally clear. At nearly six hundred metres, it is the deepest lake in the United States.

The Klamath people witnessed the eruption, and their stories of a battle between the spirits of the sky and the underworld may preserve a memory of it. The lake remains sacred to them. Wizard Island, a small cinder cone, rises from the western part of the lake, and a boat tour runs out there in summer, descending by a steep trail from Cleetwood Cove, the only legal access to the water. The park was established in 1902, one of the oldest in the country, and the area is rich in old-growth forest, with mountain hemlock, whitebark pine and wildflower meadows.

The Rim Drive circles the lake for about fifty kilometres, climbing and dipping along the crest at heights between two thousand and two and a half thousand metres. It is slower and more varied than you might expect, with a series of overlooks where you can stop. Corners are gentle, the surface is generally good, and the main hazards are tourists and cyclists, gravel on the verges, and wildlife. Snow lingers so long that the full drive usually opens only in July and closes in October, and it can close at any time after an early storm, so check the park's conditions before riding.

Fuel inside the park is limited. There is a seasonal station at Mazama Village, but it is wise to arrive with a full tank, and the nearest larger services are on the surrounding highways, at Fort Klamath, Union Creek or the Diamond Lake area. Nights are cold, even in summer, so bring layers, and the air is thin at this altitude. Smoke from wildfires can blur the view in late summer, so a clear day in July or September is best. Take your time at the overlooks, because the colour of the water changes with the light.
t.brookings@42.1,-124.3:
Brookings is the first Oregon town you meet coming up Highway 101 from California, and it greets you with unusual warmth. A quirk of the terrain and the warm winds that come down the Chetco River valley make it the mildest spot on the Oregon coast, nicknamed the banana belt, with winter temperatures that are several degrees above anywhere nearby. That climate suits flowers. More than ninety per cent of the Easter lily bulbs grown in the country come from fields around here, and in early summer the farms along the road are a sea of white trumpets.

The town has about six and a half thousand people, a working fishing harbour at the mouth of the Chetco, and a certain unfussy charm. It has one odd claim to fame: in September 1942, a Japanese submarine surfaced offshore, and a floatplane flew over the forests and dropped incendiary bombs near Mount Emily. It was the only aerial bombing of the mainland United States in the war, and the fires did little damage in the damp forest. Decades later the pilot, Nobuo Fujita, returned to Brookings as a guest, presented the town with his family's samurai sword, and planted a tree near the site as a gesture of reconciliation.

For riders, the real treat lies just north. The Samuel H. Boardman scenic corridor runs for some twelve miles along the cliffs, where the highway weaves through spruce and hemlock forest and a series of turn-offs lead to dramatic views of sea stacks, arches and hidden beaches. t.florence oregon@44.0,-124.1:

t.avenue of the giants@40.4,-123.9:

t.crescent city@41.8,-124.2:

t.newport oregon@44.6,-124.1:

t.lava beds@41.7,-121.5:

t.gold beach@42.4,-124.4:

t.eureka@40.8,-124.2:

t.diamond lake@43.2,-122.1:

t.mount shasta@41.3,-122.3:

t.toketee falls@43.3,-122.4:

t.bumpass hell@40.5,-121.5:

t.lassen peak trailhead@40.5,-121.5:

t.dee wright observatory@44.3,-121.8:

t.mckenzie bridge@44.2,-122.2:

t.santiam pass@44.4,-121.9:

t.humboldt redwoods state park@40.3,-124.0:
Ride into the redwoods from the bright, dry, noisy world of Highway 101 and the first thing that changes is the sound. Everything goes muffled. Humboldt Redwoods State Park holds tens of thousands of acres of forest along the South Fork of the Eel River, and its Rockefeller Forest is usually described as the largest surviving stretch of old-growth coast redwood anywhere. The trees are older than most European cathedrals and much taller, and the light under them is green and slow, with ferns and sorrel carpeting the floor.

The Avenue of the Giants is the old route of the highway through this country, about thirty-one miles of two-lane road that runs parallel to the freeway and weaves among the trunks. On a motorcycle it is a lovely, easygoing ride rather than a fast one. The bends are gentle, the surface is mostly good, though tree roots heave the edges in places, and the speed limit is low. The main hazards are tourists wandering in the road to photograph the trunks, and the patches of shade that stay damp after rain. Mornings can be foggy and cold, while afternoons may be warm and bright, so wear layers.

The story of the park is a conservation one. In the early twentieth century, as logging pushed up the coast, a group of well-off Californians formed the Save the Redwoods League to buy groves before the saws arrived. The state park grew out of their work, and the Rockefeller name belongs to a large donation in the 1930s. Floods on the Eel River have repeatedly swept through, and you can see high-water marks on the trunks. Roosevelt elk graze in the open meadows in places, and the salmon that run up the river in autumn are a reminder of the whole web of life here.

There is camping in the park and a visitor centre at Weott, but fuel is a different question. Rio Dell and Fortuna to the north have petrol, and Garberville to the south has more, so fill up before you enter. Food is scarce along the Avenue, with small cafes and stores in villages like Myers Flat. Mobile signal is patchy among the trees, so plan ahead.
t.founders grove@40.4,-123.9:
Founders Grove is the short walk that most people take when they only have twenty minutes, and it works. A flat loop trail threads among some of the biggest redwoods on the Avenue of the Giants, and most of them are the kind of trunks you cannot get your arms around even if five friends join in. The grove is named for the founders of the Save the Redwoods League, the group of conservationists who started buying up groves in the 1910s to rescue them from the logging that was devouring the coast.

The main attraction used to be the Dyerville Giant, a redwood that stood more than 360 feet tall, thought to be roughly sixteen centuries old. In March 1991 it fell during a storm, and it now lies along the path with its root plate towering above you like a wall of tangled earth. Walking along its length takes a while, and gives a much clearer idea of the scale than looking up at a living tree.

For a rider this is a leg-stretching stop on a road that is good for slow thought. The Avenue is tree-lined, quiet, and rarely above moderate speed, so the point is to arrive relaxed. Park on the gravel, lock your helmet to the bike, and carry a lightweight jacket. It is often cooler and damper in the grove than on the road, and in summer fog may hang overhead until late morning. The ground can be slippery, and boots with a decent sole help.

Redwoods have shallow roots, which is why they cluster and why storms bring them down, and the forest floor is a record of that: fallen logs, new trunks sprouting from old stumps, and mushrooms in the wet months. Banana slugs, bright yellow and unbothered, creep across the trail in damp weather. There are no services at the grove itself. Fortuna, about thirty-four kilometres north, and Garberville to the south have fuel, and a few small stores around Myers Flat and Weott sell drinks and snacks. Do fill the tank before starting down the Avenue.
t.mont saint michel and its bay@48.6,-1.5:
The tide here is one of the great shows of Europe. In the bay of Mont-Saint-Michel the sea can retreat for kilometres and return with a speed that has caught out many walkers, and at the biggest tides the difference between high and low water is around fourteen metres. On those days the mount, a rocky island crowned with a Benedictine abbey, can be surrounded by water, or stand alone on a plain of wet sand, depending on the hour. The causeway that used to link it to the shore has been replaced by a bridge so that the water can flow freely again.

The abbey, which took shape over a thousand years, is a mix of Romanesque and Gothic, with a spire topped by a golden statue of the archangel Michael. Its great medieval buildings on the north side are called La Merveille, the marvel. Pilgrims have come since the eighth century, when, according to tradition, Bishop Aubert founded a sanctuary after the archangel appeared to him in a dream. The border between Normandy and Brittany runs along the Couesnon river, a few kilometres away, and local people like to say that the river, in its mad moments, put the mount in Normandy.

Riding to the bay is easy, along flat roads through polders and fields where sheep graze on salt meadows, the origin of the prized pré-salé lamb. Wind and rain from the Channel can blow in fast, so keep a waterproof close, and avoid walking onto the sand without a guide, because the quicksand and fast tide are dangerous. Motorbikes are normally directed to their own parking area, and from there you walk or take the shuttle.

Pontorson, with about four thousand people, is the nearest town with fuel, supermarkets and hotels. The village at the foot of the mount has restaurants serving the famous omelettes, though they are expensive, and the local cider and calvados are much better value. Go in early morning or at dusk when the crowds thin and the light on the sand turns pink, and the ride to the D-Day beaches beyond makes a fitting contrast.
t.confluence des trois rivieres@47.6,-2.9:
The Gulf of Morbihan is a small sea, mor bihan in Breton, almost closed off from the Atlantic by a narrow gap at the entrance, and filled with islands: some say there are as many as there are days in the year, though the count depends on the tide. Water pours in and out through the narrows with such force that the current can run at several knots, and the shores are a patchwork of oyster beds, salt marshes and little harbours. The points where rivers meet the gulf, like this one, are lively places, full of birds, and shaped by the tides.

The prehistoric monuments are the other big attraction. This part of Brittany is rich in megaliths, and the cairn of Gavrinis, on an island in the gulf, has walls carved with swirling patterns that are over five thousand years old. Carnac, with its famous alignments of standing stones, lies a short ride to the north-west. The rides that start here often pass through both worlds, sea and stone.

The roads on the Rhuys peninsula, where Arzon and Larmor-Baden lie, are flat, quiet and pleasant, with views of the water from time to time and small villages of low white houses with grey slate roofs. Wind from the Atlantic is constant, and it can bring sudden showers, followed by bright light. Spring and early autumn are the best seasons, when the crowds have gone and the oysters are good.

Arzon, with about two thousand people, and Larmor-Baden have shops and cafes, but for fuel and a bigger choice, aim for Vannes, which is on the north side of the gulf and has a fine old town with medieval walls and half-timbered houses. Eat oysters and mussels, followed by a crêpe or a galette of buckwheat, with a bowl of the local cider. Ferries run to the islands from Larmor-Baden and Vannes, but they carry people, not bikes, so leave the machine on the quay and enjoy the crossing.
t.ancien moulin de moidrey@48.6,-1.5:
If you have ever seen a photograph of Mont-Saint-Michel standing alone over flat green fields, with a small windmill in the foreground, there is a fair chance it was taken here. Moidrey is a village on the Couesnon, close to Pontorson, and its old mill stands in the polders that were reclaimed from the bay over centuries. The mount sits on the horizon, a few kilometres off, shrunk to the size of a thumbnail and a little unreal, and in the early morning when mist lies in the hollows it floats above the grass.

The flat fields here are the opposite of the dramatic island, and that is what makes them so good for a pause. Sheep graze on the salt meadows, hedges mark the fields, and drainage ditches run straight toward the sea. The Couesnon, whose mouth was tamed with a dam in the twentieth century, is the border between Normandy and Brittany, and the river's history of changing course is part of local legend. The mill itself is a modest stone tower, and the view is the draw.

Riding here is simple and relaxed. The small roads between Pontorson and the bay are straight and flat, and the traffic is mostly local, with farm vehicles and cyclists. In summer the main road to the mount is busy, so the back lanes are better. Wind off the Channel can blow hard across the polders, and rain can come in quickly, so a waterproof is wise.

Pontorson, with about four thousand people, is the town for fuel, bakeries and a bed, and Roz-sur-Couesnon is a smaller village nearer the coast. Eat the lamb raised on the salt meadows, and drink the local cider, dry and cloudy. The route from here heads east across Normandy to the D-Day beaches, so the day begins with a medieval dream and ends with twentieth-century history, which is a strong pairing. Stop at the mill at dawn or dusk, and bring a good camera, but also take a minute to look without one.
t.grande mosquee de kong@9.1,-4.6:
In the north of Côte d'Ivoire, in a savanna country of scattered shea trees and red earth, the town of Kong has a past out of proportion to its size. In the eighteenth century it became the centre of the Kong empire, a Muslim-led state of Dyula traders that controlled routes for kola, gold, cloth and salt, and it grew into a famous seat of learning, with Quranic schools and libraries that were known across West Africa. The Great Mosque, built in the Sudanese style of mud, with wooden beams jutting from the walls and buttressed towers rising like pale fingers, is its monument. It belongs to the group of Sudanese-style mosques of northern Côte d'Ivoire that UNESCO inscribed in 2021.

The building itself is a lesson in clever materials. Walls of banco, mud mixed with straw and shaped by hand, are replastered each year after the rains, a community effort that renews both the mosque and the bonds of the people who maintain it. The protruding timbers, called toron, serve as permanent scaffolding. Inside, the prayer hall is cool and dim, with forests of squat mud pillars. Remember that this is a working mosque, so dress modestly and ask before entering, and avoid prayer times.

Riding up here from the south is a long day of flat savanna roads, with heat, red dust and the harmattan haze of the dry season from December to February. The main routes can be fast but cratered, and trucks and shared taxis share the tarmac with goats, cattle and the occasional pedestrian. The rains from May to October soften unpaved tracks to slippery clay. Late afternoon light on the mud walls, deep orange against a dark blue sky, is wonderful.

Kong's history has a sad chapter. In the 1890s the town was burned during the wars of the conqueror Samori Touré, and parts of its learned heritage were lost. What remains today feels quiet and dignified. Services are basic, and no nearby town was listed within range, so plan to buy fuel in larger places such as Ferkessédougou or Korhogo before arriving. Carry water, snacks and small cash, and expect any meal to be rice, grilled chicken, or a thick peanut sauce, hot with pepper.
t.petite mosquee de kong@9.1,-4.6:
Kong once had many mosques, and the small one is the better way to understand the town. Smaller than the Great Mosque, built in the same mud-and-timber tradition, it suggests how Islam here was not just a matter of grand monuments but of neighbourhoods, each with its prayer place and teacher. The Dyula, the Muslim merchants who made Kong a trading power in the eighteenth century, carried both goods and learning along the old routes from the Niger bend to the forest, and the town became a place where scholars copied books and taught the Quran.

The country around is wide, warm savanna, with red laterite roads, scattered shea and néré trees and fields of yam, millet and cotton. Riding up from the south, you notice the change from the humid forest belt to drier, more open land, and the light becomes harder and the horizons larger. The roads are usually adequate on the main routes and rough on side tracks, with potholes, speed bumps in the villages, and heavy trucks to watch for. The best time is the cooler dry season from November to February, though harmattan dust can dim the sun, and the rains from May to October make tracks muddy and rivers high.

To the east lies Comoé National Park, one of the largest protected areas in West Africa, where savanna merges into gallery forest along the Comoé river and elephants, hippos, buffalo, many antelope species and a wealth of birds make their home. It is easy to see why the park and the old Muslim town were put together in one journey, as both are about a way of living with this land. The mosques of Kong, with their rough mud surfaces, seem to grow from the same soil as the savanna itself.

For practical purposes, Kong is small and services are basic. Take fuel from a bigger town beforehand, such as Ferkessédougou or Korhogo, and carry water and food. A visit to the mosque should be arranged politely, preferably with a local person who can introduce you, and with modest dress, covered shoulders and knees. Ask before taking photographs, avoid prayer times, and consider leaving a small contribution towards the upkeep of the building. The yearly replastering of the mud is paid for by the community.
The Mont-Saint-Michel is a rock that thinks it is a cathedral. It rises from a flat bay of sand and silt on the border between Normandy and Brittany, crowned by an abbey whose spire is topped by a golden statue of the Archangel Michael. According to the old story, the archangel appeared to a bishop of Avranches in the early eighth century and told him to build a sanctuary on the rock, and Benedictine monks settled there in the tenth century. The abbey that grew over the next centuries became one of the great pilgrimage sites of medieval Europe.

The bay is the real star. The tides here are among the biggest in Europe, with a difference of up to fourteen metres between low and high water, and when the sea comes in at spring tides, it advances across the flats faster than a person can comfortably walk. The ground is soft, with patches of quicksand, and crossing it on foot is something to do only with a guide. The causeway that once connected the rock to the mainland was replaced by a bridge in 2014, and the river Couesnon now flows more freely around the base.

Cars and motorcycles are kept away from the island itself, parked at a large lot on the mainland, and shuttles carry visitors to the entrance. The nearest small village, Roz-sur-Couesnon, is about eight kilometres away, and Avranches, the nearest larger town, is thirteen. Fuel is best found at Avranches or Pontorson, and it is wise to top up before you arrive.

The area around is flat and open, with marshy meadows where salt-grazed lamb grazes, and the road along the bay offers wide views and a constant wind. Come early or late to avoid the crowds, and the place changes: the lanes empty, the light goes pink on the walls, and the sea breathes in and out beyond the sand. It is a long way from the corners of the Alps, but the sense of occasion is remarkable.
t.la citadelle el l enceinte de saint mart:
Saint-Martin-de-Ré is the fortress-town of the Île de Ré, a flat, sunny island off La Rochelle that you reach by a long bridge, built in 1988, for which a toll is charged. The harbour at Saint-Martin is a classic: stone quays, small boats, cafés and shuttered houses facing the water. Behind it rise the walls and bastions designed by Vauban for Louis XIV, which form part of the UNESCO listing of his fortifications, with a citadel that held prisoners awaiting transport to the penal colonies of Guiana.

The island is a gentle place to ride. It is about thirty kilometres long and flat, with salt marshes, oyster beds, vineyards, and villages of low whitewashed houses with pale-blue or green shutters and hollyhocks growing against the walls. Cycle paths run everywhere, and in summer the roads are packed with cyclists and cars. Speeds are low and the pleasure lies in the light, the smell of salt and pine, and the sight of egrets standing in the marshes.

There are a few quirks. Donkeys on the island once wore little trousers to protect them from insects, and the tradition lives on as a tourist attraction. Fuel is available on the island, but prices are higher, and most visitors fill up in La Rochelle before the bridge. Nieul-sur-Mer, on the mainland, is the nearest town of any size, but Saint-Martin itself has about 2,800 people and plenty of shops and restaurants.

The best time is spring or autumn, when the crowds are thin and the weather is mild. In July and August the island is full, and parking is scarce, and traffic into the harbour crawls. Park on the edge, walk through the old streets, and find a terrace overlooking the water. The oysters here are good, the white wine from the island is crisp, and the sea air will sharpen your appetite.
t.bend oregon@44.1,-121.3:
Bend sits on the dry east side of the Cascades, where the rain shadow of the volcanoes gives way to ponderosa pine, juniper and sagebrush. The Deschutes River runs through the middle of town, and on one side of the city rises Pilot Butte, a cinder cone you can drive up for a view of the Three Sisters and the rest of the range to the west. The elevation is around 3,600 feet, so the air is thin and clear, and the sun is strong even in winter.

The town began as a timber and milling center, and the old mill smokestacks still stand in the Old Mill District, where shops and restaurants now line the riverbank. It has since grown into one of the great outdoor towns of the Northwest, with more than eighty thousand people, a famous craft beer scene and a population that skis in the morning and rafts in the afternoon. Mt. Bachelor, the nearby ski mountain, draws snow lovers for much of the year. For a rider, that means good breakfasts, gear shops and every kind of fuel station.

The Cascade Lakes Scenic Byway, Highway 46, is the reason to start here. It heads southwest out of Bend, climbing past Mt. Bachelor and then winding through a string of alpine lakes including Sparks, Elk and Devils Lake, with views of the volcanoes at nearly every bend. The road is smooth and well graded, with gentle curves and good sight lines, and it passes through lodgepole forest and old lava flows. The Lava Butte area south of town has a cinder cone and a lava flow you can walk across, and the Lava Lands visitor center is a useful stop.

Timing is crucial. The byway is closed in winter beyond the Mt. Bachelor turnoff, usually from around November until late spring or early summer, depending on snow. Summer is the best season, though mosquitoes can be thick near the lakes in June and July, and weekend traffic is heavy at the trailheads. Mornings are chilly even in August, so bring a warm layer.

Fuel stations thin out as you leave town, so top up before you climb. Sunriver has services, but there is little along the lakes beyond a handful of lodges and small stores.
t.kohm yah mah nee visitor center@40.4,-12:
The name is Maidu, from the people who lived on these slopes long before anyone surveyed them, and it means Snow Mountain. Kohm Yah-mah-nee is the visitor centre at the southwest entrance of Lassen Volcanic National Park in northern California, a modern building of stone and timber set among tall conifers. It is a good first stop for the road through the park: you can look at the displays, ask the rangers about conditions on the upper road, and take a look at a model of the volcano before you see the real thing.

Lassen Peak is the southernmost volcano of the Cascade chain, the same line that holds Mount St. Helens, Rainier and Hood. It is a lava dome, one of the largest of its kind in the world, and it erupted repeatedly between 1914 and 1917, throwing ash across the region and flattening forest on its flank. That activity led to the creation of the park in 1916. Around it, you can still find steaming vents, bubbling mud pots and turquoise lakes, with Bumpass Hell, the largest hydrothermal area in the park, a short hike from the road.

The park highway crosses the whole area in about thirty miles, climbing past meadows and volcanic rubble to a high point of around eighty-five hundred feet, then dropping toward the north. It is smooth, with easy bends, wide pull-outs and plenty of views, and traffic is light compared with better-known parks. Because of the heavy snowfall, the upper road is closed for much of the year, typically from late autumn until late spring or early summer, and snowbanks can still line it in June, so check the status first.

Services are limited. Pack lunch, water and a warm layer. The air smells of sulphur near the thermal areas and of resin among the pines, and mosquitoes can be thick in the wet meadows in early summer. Autumn is lovely, with golden light and few visitors, and the road can be a pleasure to ride when the weather holds.
t.manzanita lake@40.5,-121.6:
Manzanita Lake is the postcard of Lassen Volcanic National Park, and on a calm morning the reflection is hard to ignore. The water is shallow and still, edged with reeds and conifers, and the pale cone of Lassen Peak sits upside down in it, flanked by the broken crags of Chaos Crags. A flat path loops the lake, and the northwest entrance station is only a short distance away. Most people come early in the day for the still air and soft light, and the mirror-like surface.

The odd name for the crags is deserved. Around three hundred years ago, a series of lava domes collapsed, sending avalanches of rock racing down the slope and across the land below. The debris field, known as the Chaos Jumbles, is a jumble of boulders scattered in a wide fan, now covered in sparse forest. It is a reminder that the volcanic story here is far from over, and the park lies on a restless part of the Cascade range.

The historic Loomis Museum, a stone building beside the lake, is named after a local photographer who recorded the 1914 to 1917 eruptions of Lassen Peak, and his images are among the best records of the event. A small ranger station and cabins by the lake keep the place feeling like a classic national park of the early twentieth century, with a camp store that opens in the season.

As a rider, this is the finish of a long and beautiful day, and the road north of the park runs downhill through ponderosa pine and open woods, in sweeping descents and relaxed bends. The air at this elevation, about fifty-eight hundred feet, is clear and dry, and evenings are cool. Services are limited, so fuel should be bought outside, at Shingletown or at Chester, both a good distance away, and it is wise to leave the park with a full tank. Summer weekends can be busy, and the best moments are in September, when the crowds have gone and the light turns golden. Bears live in the park, so store food carefully, and keep a sharp eye out for deer at dawn and dusk.
t.phillipsville@40.2,-123.8:
Phillipsville is one of the first doorways into the Avenue of the Giants, and it announces the change in a gentle way. The little community, a few buildings at a turn-off from the main highway, is where the old road leaves the freeway and ducks beneath the redwoods. Within a mile, the light changes from bright sun to a deep green dusk, the air cools, and the smell of damp earth and resin takes over. The trees are enormous, with trunks wider than your garage, and they rise beyond sight.

The coast redwood, Sequoia sempervirens, is the tallest tree on Earth, with the biggest individuals reaching over three hundred and fifty feet, and they live for well over a thousand years. This grove forms part of Humboldt Redwoods State Park, which protects some of the largest stands of old-growth redwood left, saved by conservation groups in the 1920s, after they realised that loggers were cutting them down at astonishing speed. Fog drifting in from the Pacific supplies much of the moisture the trees need during the dry summer.

The Avenue itself is a thirty-one-mile ribbon of old highway that runs beside the freeway, along the south fork of the Eel River. It is narrow and curving, with a few tight spots, and the surface is rough in places where roots have heaved the asphalt. The speed limit is low, and rightly so, since the trees come up to the edge of the road, shadows fall in patches, and cyclists and sightseers often stop without warning. It is best taken slowly, with frequent stops to walk among the trunks, and the early morning light slanting through the mist is magical.

Fuel is easy to find at Redway and Garberville, a short distance to the south, and it is wise to fill up before entering the grove. A number of roadside stands sell burls and carvings, and a few of the old tourist attractions, such as drive-through trees, are still running. It can be cool and damp even in summer, and winter brings heavy rain and the occasional flood, so be ready with waterproofs. Spring and autumn are quieter, and the redwood forest is at its most atmospheric when mist hangs among the trunks.
t.pepperwood@40.4,-124.0:
Pepperwood is another name for the California bay laurel, a tree whose leaves smell sharp and peppery when crushed, and the little community that took it as a name sits at the northern end of the Avenue of the Giants. It is a scatter of houses and a few farm buildings beside the Eel River, with redwoods behind and a flat river bottom in front, and it marks the point where the old highway meets the freeway again after its slow journey through the giants.

The area has a heavy history of timber. The big lumber company that owned much of this land built the nearby town of Scotia, one of the last company towns in America, with a mill on the river that processed redwood for decades. Houses were rented to workers, and a company store and a hall stood at the centre. You can still see the mill, and a small museum tells the story of the logging era, with its saws, teams and railways. The scale of the cutting explains why people fought to save what remains.

Floods have also shaped the valley. The Eel River is prone to dramatic winter floods, and in 1955 and 1964 great surges of water tore through the redwood groves, carrying away bridges, houses and even huge trees. High-water marks are painted on buildings in some places, and they climb well above head height, a vivid reminder of the forces at work in this landscape. In summer, the river drops to a gentle trickle, with gravel bars and swimming holes, and the valley feels peaceful.

The riding here is a gentle way to end the journey. The road runs close to the river, in easy curves with the trees thinning to open farmland and the hills of the Coast Range ahead. Traffic is light, but log trucks and sightseers are common. Rio Dell, a few kilometres on, has fuel and a few places to eat, and Fortuna, a larger town, has more stations, supermarkets and motels. The weather is mild and often foggy, particularly in the morning, and the climate is cool even in summer, so a jacket is useful. Spring brings wildflowers and green hillsides, while autumn is calm.
